Jampa Gyeltsen Lhalungpa (lha lung pa byams pa rgyal mtshan) was born in 1921 in Lhasa into the Lhalung family (lha lung tshang) which descends from Lhalung Pelgyi Dorje (lha lung dpal gyi rdo rje), the purported assassin of King Langdarma (glang dar ma, r. 841–842). He was the eldest son of Gyeltsen Tarchin Lhalungpa (lha lung pa rgyal mtshan mthar phyin), who served as the Nechung Oracle from 1913 to 1915. Gyeltsen Tarchin, known also as Chozur Lhalungpa (chos zur lha lung pa) or Kungo Chozur (sku ngo cho zur), was removed from his position owing to a dispute over funds at Nechung. According to the account given by Jampa Gyeltsen's brother Lobsang Phuntsok Lhalungpa (lha lung pa blo bzang phun tshogs, 1926-2008) to Polish scholar René de Nebesky-Wojkowitz (1923-1959), and recorded in his book Oracles and Demons, monks at Nechung disagreed with the management of funds by Gyeltsen Tarchin's father, who was secretary for his son. The government then dismissed him from his post, in which he had served for around two years.[1] In the oral history taken by Melvyn Goldstein and Tashi Tsering, Jampa Gyeltsen remarked that there was a ""case"" but gave no further detail.

According to Lobsang Phuntsok Lhalungpa, the government actually offered the Nechung Oracle position to his father again after a period of time. However, Chozur Lhalungpa had by then disrobed and married. Despite these events, Gyeltsen Tarchin remained on good terms with the Thirteenth Dalai Lama, Tubten Gyatso (ta la'i bla ma 13 thub bstan rgya mtsho, 1876-1933).

At some point, the Dalai Lama gave Chozur Lhalungpa the Lhasa household and nearby Dakpo estates of the Drumpa family (bhrum pa). This family had become allied with the family of the Thirteenth Dalai Lama in the late nineteenth century when the Dalai Lama's elder brother, Langdun Lobzang Tashi (glang mdun blo bzang bkra shis, 18th-19th century), took over the household. His son, Namgyel Gyeltsen (rnam rgyal rgyal mtshan, 1898–1930), succeeded as head of the household but died in 1930.[2] Because Jampa Gyeltsen's family was associated with the Drumpas, he was nicknamed Drumpa but did not use the name formally.[3]

Jampa Gyeltsen and his brother, Lobsang Phuntsok Lhalungpa, began their education together in the secular schools of Lhasa, first at the Yulkhagang School (g.yul kha sgang slob grwa). At the age of ten, he entered Loseling College (blo gsal gling grwa tshang) of Drepung Monastery ('bras spungs dgon), receiving preliminary ordination and joining the Gyelrong Khamtsen (rgyal rong khams mtshan), or Gyelrong Residential House. After residing at the monastery for a few months, Jampa Gyeltsen and Lobsang Phuntsok returned to their Lhasa home and continued their studies at the Nyarongsha School (nyag rong shag slob grwa), which had been established in the 1920s on property donated by the Surkhang family (zur khang). In their teenage years, the brothers began intensive studies under the guidance of a private tutor, Pemachok Pelzangpo (pad+ma mchog dpal bzang po, 1914–1963), a scholar from Tashilhunpo Monastery (bkra shis lhun po). After studying at the Nyarongsha school, Jampa Gyeltsen entered the Tse Lobdra (rtse slob grwa), the school for monk officials, where he studied for a year and a half. In 1938, at the age of sixteen, Jampa Gyeltsen became a monk official, or tsedrung (rtse drung), working in the secretariat of the Dalai Lama (rtse yig tshang or rtse gag).

He worked in the office for several years. In his first few months, his main responsibility was attending the drungja (drung ja), or morning tea meeting at the Tse Yiktsang. Later his work revolved around writing edicts and other documents. Within a few years he was appointed as caretaker of Serdong Pende Wobar (gser sdong phan bde'i 'od 'bar) at the Potala (po ta la), a golden stūpa that held the remains of the Eleventh Dalai Lama, Khedrub Gyatso (ta la'i bla ma 11 rgyal ba mkhas grub rgya mtsho, 1938–1855). Around this time he also assisted Mindrukbuk Tubten Gyelpo (smin drug sbug thub bstan rgyal po po, b. 1903), his music teacher and Yiktsang Secretary (yig tshang gnyer pa), in producing folk operas, particularly for the annual festival held each September in Lhasa.

In 1946, Jampa Gyeltsen joined the staff of Lhalu Tsewang Dorje (lha klu tshe dbang rdo rje, 1914–2011), who was cabinet minister, or kalon (bka' blon) from 1946 to 1952, and also governor of Kham (mdo smad spyi khyab). As a part of Lhalu's staff, Jampa Gyeltsen left Lhasa for Kham, and was stationed in Chamdo at a time when the Chinese forces were encroaching on Tibetan territories. In 1950 he was part of a troop of Khampas in Denma (ldan ma) attempting to defend the area from oncoming Chinese troops. Within a few days they were outnumbered, Jampa Gyeltsen was arrested, and all his belongings were taken. He slowly made his way back to Lhasa on foot as though on a pilgrimage, arriving in the early 1950s.[4] By this time, his brother Lobsang Phuntsok was in India, having left Tibet in 1947 to teach at St. Joseph's College. When the Preparatory Committee of the Tibetan Autonomous Region (bod rang skyong ljong gra sgrigs u yon lhan khang, PCTAR) was established in 1956, he was ordered to work as a printer, owing to his previous experience in painting. Each month he earned seventy dayang (da yang), a silver coin in circulation at the time.

By the late 1950's the situation in Lhasa had grown increasingly tense, culminating in the March Tenth uprising of 1959 and the Fourteenth Dalai Lama's flight to India. Jampa Gyeltsen was part of a group defending the Jokhang (jo khang) and was arrested for his role in the resistance. He spent the next twenty-two years imprisoned, though he was never given a definite sentence. He recalled how he was repeatedly told his release was imminent, only to remain in custody. Jampa Gyeltsen was first held in Taring prison, and later at a prison at Drakri Hermitage (brag ri ri khrod) where he worked as a cook.

He was finally released in December 1981, returning to Lhasa to find that many members of his family had been tortured or killed, his father's home had been confiscated and the family's estate outside of the city was in ruins. His monastery of Drepung suffered as well. He himself also experienced lasting physical effects of imprisonment, having suffered from malnourishment and physical labors. At some point he suffered a minor stroke.

Once back in Lhasa, Jampa Gyeltsen had no home to return to. He was allowed to live on the grounds of the Lukhang (klu khang), where he acted as caretaker. He resided with his sister, a nun, named Ani Jampa Dolkar (a ni byams pa sgrol dkar). He began an informal school on Lukhang grounds for children who would have otherwise lacked access to Tibetan education. He taught his students reading, writing, and liturgy and survived on his small caretaker salary and food donations from students' families. A former student remembered large groups of children in attendance, as many as one hundred. Jampa Gyeltsen was a strict disciplinarian and used traditional methods of education including wooden boards for writing instruction and even occasional corporal punishment. Jampa Gyeltsen's nephew Samphe Lhalungpa, son of Lobsang Phuntsok Lhalungpa, remembers his father telling him that Ngapo Ngawang Jigme (nga phod ngag dbang 'jigs med, 1910–2009) visited the school and commended Jampa Gyeltsen on his work.[5]

In 1982, Jampa Gyeltsen was visited by his brother, who by this time had relocated to the United States; Lobsang Phuntsok had not visited Tibet since leaving in 1947. The two brothers had corresponded over the years, their letters now preserved in the private papers of Lobsang Phuntsok Lhalungpa.

Jampa Gyeltsen is cited in a Tibet Information Network (TIN) News Review from 26 April 1994 in the context of government shutdowns of private schools. It notes that Jampa Gyeltsen reportedly refused entry to Chinese journalists and subsequently was investigated, eventually leading to the closure of the school and transfer of his students to a government school. In this report it states that he died of a heart attack several days after the school closed. He was in the company of his sister, Ani Jampa Dolkar, at the time of his death on 10 March 1993. He was 72 years old.

Karma Chopel was a doctor of traditional Tibetan medicine who trained under Khyenrab Norbu at the Mentsikhang in Lhasa, where he later served as head of the medical research department. He taught in the Tibetan Medicine Department at the Tibet University and traveled internationally to speak on Tibetan medicine.

","

Karma Chopel (kar+ma chos 'phel) was born to a father named Samten (bsam gtan) and a mother Chungkyi (chung skyid) in Zhuto Tashi Gang (zhu stod bkra shis sgang) in Nyemo (snye mo), central Tibet, in 1930. His family took pride in its strong connection to the medical profession and counted the famed physician-scholar Konchok Dropen Wangpo (dkon mchog 'gro phan dbang po, b. 1631) among its forefathers. Tubten Kunpel (thub bstan kun 'phel, 1905–1963), the attendant to the Thirteenth Dalai Lama, Tubten Gyatso (tA la'i bla ma 13 thub bstan rgya mtsho, 1876–1933), was one of Karma Chopel's cousins. His family owned a rich collection of medical and astrological texts and equipment collected and preserved by his forefathers over the centuries. Growing up in a family that valued the medical profession, Karma Chopel enjoyed roleplaying as a physician even from a very young age.

In 1936, the six-year Karma Chopel studied reading and writing under his uncle at Tawu Sangngak Chokdrub Ling (rta'u gsang sngags mchog grub gling), a Drigung Kagyu monastery in Zhuto. Then, in 1942, he became a monk and formally joined the monastery. A year later, his uncle sent him to Yangpachen (yangs pa can) in Lhasa to study medicine under Pelden Gyeltsen (dpal ldan rgyal mtshan), one of Khyenrab Norbu's (mkhyen rab nor bu, 1883–1962) leading disciples. As a medical trainee and apprentice, Karma Chopel accompanied his teacher for outstation visits, including to purify mercury at Tsurpu Monastery (mtshur phu dgon) in a process presided over by the Sixteenth Karmapa Rangjung Rikpai Dorje (karma pa rang byung rig pa'i rdo rje, 1924–1981). Soon after arriving at the monastery, however, his master became ill and departed from Yangpachen for an extended religious pilgrimage. Left without a teacher, Karma Chopel returned to Tawu Monastery in 1945.

About a year later, Karma Chopel gained admission to Mentsikhang, the Tibetan Medical and Astrological Institute, also known as Lhasa Mentsi Dropen Ling (bod ljongs lha sa sman rtsis 'gro phan gling), during a selection of candidates from the local monasteries. At Mentsikhang, under Khyenrab Norbu and the resident teachers like Tukse Tubten Lhundrub (thugs sras thub bstan lhun grub, 1906–1955), Yeshe Chopel (ye shes chos 'phel), and Konchok Lhundrub (dkon mchog lhun grub), he studied and trained in astrology and medicine, including practices such as surgery, bloodletting, moxibustion, fumigation, balm-based chiropractic, and cupping. As Karma Chopel had traveled as Palden Gyaltsen’s apprentice in a mercury purification trip before, he was sent to assist Tenzin Chodrak (bstan 'dzin chos grags, 1922–2001) to learn mercury purification from Pelden Gyaltsen in Pari.

His years at Mentsikhang included, as traditional apprenticeship demanded, running errands and household chores for his teachers. As the institute provided students a monthly food supply of approximately twenty pounds, there were times when Karma Chopel ran out of food and had to borrow grain and flour from his friends and relatives.

On the fifteenth day of the third lunar month of 1950, he graduated in traditional medicine and astrology. As Mentsikhang retained students with outstanding academic excellence, Karma Chopel was offered a managerial position at the department of pharmacology. During his years, he participated in the annual medical camps to Lawok (la 'og), Lungnak Tselka (lung nag tshal ka), and Drak Yerpa (brag yer pa). First introduced and led by Desi Sangye Gyatso (sde srid sangs rgyas rgya mtsho, 1653-1705) in 1696 for Chakpori (lcags po ri), the camping involved a field study of herbs and plants and an annual exam. In 1954 and 1955, Karma Chopel excelled in the herb identification exams at these camps and was assigned a supervisory role in the subsequent camps.

Karma Chopel began his clinical practice in 1955. Under Khyenrab Norbu's initiatives, the traditional Tibetan government had founded the Beggars' House, or Trangkhang (sprang khang), in Lhasa in 1955. Also, Khyenrab Norbu instituted a mobile medical unit to visit the homes of bedridden patients, as well as attend to the homeless on the streets of Lhasa. That year, Khyenrab Norbu appointed Karma Chopel to join the clinical department. Karma Chopel dutifully assisted Khyenrab Norbu in his clinics and visits during the day and discussed the diagnoses, medications, and prognoses at the end of each day.

In June 1959, after Communist China took complete control of Tibet, the medical unit of the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) in Lhasa reached out to Mentsikhang for the service of a Tibetan medical physician. Khyenrab Norbu delegated Karma Chopel for this task. The same month Karma Chopel joined a five-member Chinese medical team led by Yang Fuxing 楊福興 and surveyed the regions of Powo (spo bo), Nyingtri (nying khri), and Menlung (sman lung) for medicinal herbs and plants. At the unit, Karma Chopel saw patients from the PLA force, particularly the Tibetan division.

The following year, when China's central botanical institute explored and surveyed Tibet’s vegetation geography and studied its plant species, Karma Chopel joined a seventeen-member team as a Tibetan expert and toured Tibetan regions designated within the Tibetan Autonomous Region (TAR) for nearly four months.

Upon his return, he also worked at Hospital No. 49, which housed patients with illnesses that were unresponsive to allopathic medicine. For example, the hospital was once flooded by hundreds of Chinese soldiers with severe frostbite during their mission to fight Tibetan resistance forces in the northern regions (byang khul). While Karma Chopel had no experience treating such cases, he sought guidance from Khyenrab Norbu, who had treated such patients in the past. With his master's instructions, the medical authorities there first assigned thirty patients for treatment. It is said that in a matter of days, the patients whose limbs and fingers had severely numbed and hardened gradually began to heal. He was successful in eventually treating all patients and saving many from amputation. Also, working with other Chinese medical professionals, Karma Chopel learned the Chinese language, allopathy and Chinese traditional medicine, and medical and botanical terms in Latin.

In 1961, the military authorities of the Tibetan division of the PLA ordered the construction of a Tibetan medicine production unit at Gyechik (brgyad gcig) in Nyingtri. Karma Chopel and a nineteen-member team oversaw the construction by local Tibetan laborers. The unit opened the following year, yet rather than being dedicated to Tibetan medicine it was used for the production of Huangliansu 黃連素 pills made from berberis (skyer pa) and packaging, likely by hand, APC tablets (pills comprised of aspirin, phenacetin, and caffeine).

In addition to his responsibilities at the production unit, he also saw patients at the hospital. While he initially treated new Tibetan soldiers, his fame later attracted patients from the nearby regions Powo, Menlung, and Kongpo (kong po), who were seen and treated without charge. When the hospital ran short of Tibetan medicine, it reached out to Mentsikhang and exchanged APC pills for Tibetan pills to replenish his supply.

Despite the initial plan to produce Tibetan pills, the unit continued making Huangliansu and wrapping APC pills. As Karma Chopel was also responsible for motivating Tibetans to supply medicinal roots of berberis shrub for Huangliansu production, locals knew him as Utok Emji (u tog em je), meaning ""Doctor Berberis Root.""

In 1965, when a Chinese medical team led by Dr. Xiao Bankan arrived in central Tibet, Karma Chopel joined the group and toured Dromo (gro mo), Tsona (mtsho sna), and Kyirong (skyid grong). Upon return, they published the Early Research on the Tibetan Science of Healing and Medical Substances (bod kyi gso rig dang sman rdzas la thog ma'i zhib 'jug rags tsam byas pa) in a Mentsikhang journal. It was the first publication that incorporated Western and Chinese knowledge and medical terms. In 1969, he collaborated with four Chinese physicians to publish a Sino-Tibetan comparative work on medicine.

In the summers of 1973 and 1974, he joined a fourteen-member Chinese team to survey and explore central Tibet, south-central Tibet, and the regions of Kham including Gonjo (go 'jo), Tsakalo (tshwa kha lho), Chamdo (chab mdo), and Dzayul (rdza yul) for medical plants. The information he gathered during these missions were subsequently published in research articles and materia medica.

In 1975, when Mentsikhang had used up its ash from mercury ore, Karma Chopel returned to help revive the mercury production there. The same year the medicine production unit moved from Nyingtri to Lhasa despite the opposition of locals who sought to keep Karma Chopel in the region. In Lhasa he continued seeing patients and also visited Chinese provinces to treat high-ranking patients. The same year, the medical unit for the Tibetan division of the PLA extended him the honorary title of Menram (sman rams, also sman pa rab 'byams), which is loosely equivalent to a master’s degree in medical sciences.

In 1980 he joined several editorial boards for series and books on medicine. That same year the military unit bestowed a second degree, Menpa Bumrampa Zhonpa (sman pa 'bum rams pa gzhon pa), meaning Junior Bumrampa; bumram is traditionally equivalent to a doctorate.

In 1984, as he had long desired, he was able to return to Mentsikhang and serve as the head (suo zhang 所長) of the medical research department. In addition to his research and administrative works, he also saw patients, continuing his master Khyenrab Norbu's practice of visiting bedbound and homeless patients.

In 1985, when the Tenth Paṇchen Lama, Trinle Lhundrub Chokyi Gyaltsen (phrin las lhun grub chos kyi rgyal mtshan, 1938–1989), visited Lhasa to participate in the twentieth anniversary of China's creation of the TAR, a ceremony also attended by the Chinese Premier Li Peng (1928–2019), the Chinese government appointed Karma Chopel as the official physician to the Paṇchen Lama. However, it was only a year later, that Panchen Lama, upon insistence from his family members, consulted Karma Chopel for the first time for a case of severe indigestion. Impressed by his service, the Paṇchen Lama appointed Karma Chopel his personal physician (bla sman) and availed his service during his visits to the Tibetan regions until his death in 1989.

Starting in 1985 he lectured at the newly founded Tibetan Medicine Department at the Tibet University (bod ljongs slob grwa chen mo) in Lhasa, and later at Bojong Sorik Lobling (bod ljongs gso rig slob gling) after its founding in 1989.

Karma Chopel traveled to various provinces in China. As a member of the China Tibetology Research Center, he also traveled to multiple countries, including Nepal, France, England, Switzerland, Germany, Austria, Luxemburg, and Denmark, where he gave talks and saw patients.

In 1987, the TAR honored him with Mennyer Bumram (sman gnyer 'bum rams), which is loosely equivalent to a doctorate in medicine with a focus on pharmacology. Then, in 1991, the TAR government conferred him the title of Rikchik Khechen (rigs gcig mkhas can), meaning ""expert in a field of specialization.""

He held positions including the head (wu yuan 務院) of the National Medical Association, an executive member of Tibetan Medical Association, a supervisor at the Regional Board for Medicinal Herbs and Minerals, and an editor of the board of China's Menbum (sman 'bum) publications.

He published numerous articles in Tibetan books and journals. In 1993, he published his magnum opus—The Excellent Jewel Rosary of Elegant Instructions: A Materia Medica of Ambrosial Medicine (bdud rtsi sman gyi 'khrungs dpe legs bshad nor bu'i phreng mdzes), which was an outcome of his research and data collection he began in 1973. With Chinese equivalent terms as well as western botanical and chemical names and his comparative study of earlier works, the book remains his single-most important work. As Khyenrab Norbu's famed Heart Jewel of the Youthful Physician Jivika: An Extensive Materia Medica ('khrungs dpe rgyas pa 'tsho byed gzhon nu'i snying nor) was no longer extant, Karma Chopel’s book remained one of the authoritative works that directly draws from the transmitted body of knowledge on traditional botany and pharmacology of the great master. He also wrote on related fields such as equine veterinary practice titled The Mirror: Elucidation on Horse and Equine Veterinary (rta bshad dang rta bcos gsal ba'i me long).
In 1996, as commissioned by the Chinese government, he assumed the role of editor of China’s Hundred Thousand Plants (krung hua sngo 'bum) and worked on the publication till 1998.

After over four decades of service in the fields of medicine, Karma Chopel died at the age of sixty-nine in Lhasa on August 4, 1999, following months of prolonged illness. He was survived by his wife Dolkar (sgrol dkar) and daughters Dekyi (bde skyid) and Ngodrup Wangmo (dngos grub dbang mo).

Takla Norbu was a twentieth-century Tibetan doctor. He was trained at Dodrubchen and Pelpung monasteries and practiced mainly in the Golok region. Famous for his miraculous cures, he is credited with introducing moxibustion to the region.

","

Takla Norbu (stag bla nor bu) was born in the Taktok Pon family, also known as Takleb Pon (stag thog/stag leb dpon), in Golok (mgo log), Amdo, in 1889. Born into a chieftain family with access to physicians and astrologers, the young Takla Norbuwas was able to learn reading and writing, and he enjoyed carving or inscribing designs resembling astrological signs and symbols on sticks and stones. He became a monk at a young age and received the monastic name Jigme Tubten Gyatso ('jigs med thub bstan rgya mtsho). Norbu appears to be his given name.

At the medical colleges (sman pa grwa tshang) at Dodrubchen Ngodrub Pelbar Ling (rdo grub chen dngos grub dpal 'bar gling) in Golok and Pelpung Tubten Chokhor Ling (dpal spungs thub bstan chos 'khor gling) in Derge he studied advanced linguistics, grammar, composition, religion, philosophy, medicine, and astrology, including the Indo-Tibetan planetary astrology (skar rtsis), Swarodaya astrology (dbyangs 'char), and Sino-Tibetan astrology (nag rtsis), under Ju Mipam Namgyel Gyatso ('ju mi pham rnam rgyal rgya mtsho, 1846–1912), Taktok Tsoknyi Gyatso (stag thog tshogs gnyis rgya mtsho), Chakchung Gyurme (phyag chung 'gyur med), and Pelpung Karma Trinle (dpal spungs karma 'phrin las).

Takla’s students and followers narrate some fascinating accounts recounting his power of mixing magic and astrology. Stories of how he used white magic to save animals from hunters and hunting dogs, and to intercept thieves, were popular among the locals in the Golok region. In most cases, these stories tell how he inscribed letters, numbers, and symbols on stones and sticks to produce the intended effect.

In addition to consulting him for regular natal, matrimonial, and death horoscopes, local people from all ranks of society also sought his astrological expertise for other purposes, such as predicting a prognosis, determining lifespan, retrieving lost objects, and ensuring victory in a battle. During his lifetime, he was considered one of the few astrologers who understood the intended import of the Yuddhajayārṇava-tantra, or Swarodaya Tantra on “Victory in a Battle” (g.yul las rnam par rgyal ba'i dbyangs 'char ba'i rgyud).

He was a skilled physician who excelled in all aspects of knowledge and practice of Tibetan medicine. Possessing a skill combination found in very rare cases, Takla Norbu was an expert diviner who conducted mirror divination (pra phab), chalk divination (tho le kor gyi mo pra), pulse divination (rtsa pra), and numerical divination (rtsis dpyad), and he diagnosed maladies and administered medicine through these means. His unlimited skills and knowledge of medicine and astrology earned him the byname ""The All-Knowing Physician"" (sman pa thams cad mkhyen pa). He was also praised as “the Second Yuthok” (g.yu thog gnyis pa), after Yutok Yonten Gonpo the Younger (g.yu thog gsar ma yon tan mgon po, 1126-1202), who is considered the father of Tibetan medicine.

Stories of his healing power abound. Once, in Tsang, Takla Norbu was said to have treated a pregnant woman who was presumed dead, having bled heavily and fallen unconscious during pre-delivery contractions. Seeing that she was hemorrhaging ""live blood"" (gson khrag) instead of ""post-death blood"" (shi khrag), Takla Norbu immediately administered moxibustion on her right kidney. The woman regained her senses and delivered her child. Takla's explanation was that the fetus had been in a breech position and was putting pressure on the mother's kidney with its hand. The heat from moxibustion loosened the fetus' grip and revived the mother, whereby her instinct ensured a safe delivery. Local people were said to have been convinced that he had brought the woman back from the state of death.

Active as a physician during the first half of the twentieth century, many people from regions around Golok that Takla Norbu treated experience miraculous cures from their disease, some considered congenital and severe. People were said to have regained their sight and walked after crippling diseases. He also practiced bovine and equine veterinary medicine, combining them with astrology.

He was said to have refused payments of wealth and livestock for these miraculous treatments, instead advising family members and locals to engage in religious activities, such as reciting mantras and prayers.

He was credited with introducing different combinations of herbs and plants. He published around thirty-two important texts and articles on medicine, writing on astrology and more than forty essential topics. He was also credited for popularizing bloodletting and moxibustion among the physicians of Golok in the mid-twentieth century.

Takla Norbu treated many famous Tibetan masters of his time, including the Third Dodrubchen, Tenpai Nyima (rdo grub chen 03 bstan pa'i nyi ma, 1865–1926); Pawo Choying Dorje (dpa' bo chos dbyings rdo rje, 1895–1945); Tsangpa Drubchen Jampa Chozin (gtsang pa grub chen byams pa chos 'dzin, 1830–1945); Dartang Chaktsa Jampel Lodro (dar thang phyag tsha 'jam dpal blo gros, 1892–1958/1959); and the Third Dzongnang Lama, Jampel Gyepai Dorje (rdzong nang bla ma 03 'jam dpal dgyes pa'i rdo rje, 1894–1958).

He also received teachings from these great masters, as well as scores of other masters such as the Thirteenth Dalai Lama Tubten Gyatso (tA la'i bla ma 13 thub btsan rgya mtsho, 1876–1933) and the Ninth Paṇchen Lama Tubten Chokyi Nyima (paN chen 09 thub bstan chos kyi nyi ma, 1883–1937). Similarly, he had a huge following of disciples including lamas and physicians in Amdo and Kham in the twentieth century, including Rigzin Jalu Dorje (rig 'dzin 'ja' lus rdo rje, 1927–1961), one of two men to be recognized as the Fourth Dodrubchen.

Takla Norbu undertook many medical retreats at sacred places and sites in and around the Golok region of Amdo, such as Nyenpo Yurtse (gnyan po g.yu rtse), Nechen Pema Rito (gnas chen pad+ma ri mtho), Wenri Lhachen Dong (dben ri lha chen gdong), Rabcha Gang (rab cha sgang), and Magyel Pomra (rma rgyal spom ra). As these sites are considered to have been blessed by Padmasambhava and Vairocana during their mystical visits in the eighth century, the medicinal plants and herbs in the region are unique, and the medical practice in the region is regarded as a powerful dharma practice.

Takla Norbu was also a devotee of Avalokiteśvara and was believed to have recited the six-syllable mantra several hundred million times throughout his life. He is said to have had visions of Black Garuda (mkha' lding nag po) and Dorje Yudronma (rdo rje g.yu sgron ma), as well as the three Medicine Goddesses (sman gyi lha mo.) Black Garuda is said to play a role in destroying the pestilent Nagas; Dorje Yudronma is important in mirror divination; and the Medicine Goddesses are central in the Medicine Buddha sādhanas. Later scholars and physicians eulogized Takla Norbu as an incarnation of the Medicine Buddha and of the famed Tibetan adept Drapa Ngonshe (grwa pa mngon shes, 1012–1090), who was credited for discovering the Four Tantras (rgyud bzhi), the foundation texts of the Tibetan medical tradition.

Takla Norbu died in Amdo, in the male earth-dog year during its eleventh month, which began on December 11, 1958 and ended on January 9, 1959. Throughout his life, he lived by the traditional Tibetan dictum: ""all plants are medicinal; all treatments must be altruistic,"" which directs Tibetan physicians in the same way as the Hippocratic Oath guides doctors in Western medicine.

Trinle Chodron, better known as Nyemo Ani, was a nun from a large tenant family that lived on a Lhalu estate in central Tibet. After a period of illness, she sought the assistance of a local lama and became empowered to act as a medium. She often channeled Ani Gongme Gyelmo, a spirit from the Gesar of Ling pantheon. She became known for healing and divinations at the same time as pervasive dissatisfaction with Communist reforms in her village led to factional conflict between two groups, known as Nyamdrel and Gyenlok. Becoming allied with Gyenlok, which opposed the existing Party structure, she encouraged resistance and armed attacks on local cadres that culminated in a period of violent attacks in June of 1969. She was eventually captured by PLA forces and executed in Lhasa in 1970.

","

Trinle Chodron was born around 1938 into the Peljang (spel byang) family, who were tenants, or trelpa (khral pa) on a Lhalu (lha lu) estate. Trelpa, or taxpayers, lived on estates that engaged in agricultural and other labor, paying taxes to the estate landowners. As trelpa were free to leave the estate, they were a class above the tseyok (tshe g.yog), or hereditary servants. Information about Trinle Chodron's life are found in the detailed account and analysis by Melvyn Goldstein, Ben Jiao, and Tanzen Lhundrup in On the Cultural Revolution in Tibet: On the Nyemo Incident of 1969, which draws on Chinese government reports and on extensive oral histories of Nyemo villagers including Trinle Chodron's younger brother. These oral histories are now preserved at the Library of Congress as part of the Tibetan Oral History Archive Project.

Trinle Chodron was the eldest of eleven children. She entered Taser Nunnery (mtha' ser), a Kagyu institution in Pusum (phu gsum), Nyemo (snye mo), when she was around twelve years old. Although she remained a nun after the upheaval of the Communist invasion of Tibet, she was unable to continue religious life, and instead had to work during the day. She did, however, continue to reside in a building next to the former nunnery with her teacher. She had basic reading skills.

After being abruptly forced to abandon her religious life during the onset of the Cultural Revolution in 1966, when she would have been in her late twenties, Goldstein, Jiao, and Lhudrup suggest that she was likely subjected to humiliating struggle sessions.[1] Deemed upper-middle class, her family also faced challenges such as their home being searched by Red Guards. Her teacher, who was elderly, died. These events are purported to have contributed to her mental destabilization, which was attested to by her relatives and neighbors. According to her younger brother, she would wander off for days at a time. She was regarded as mentally unwell by those around her.[2]

For years, she was known to talk to herself, imagining people in front of her and having frequent hallucinations. She also became physically ill, unable even to walk. Trinle Chodron asked her brother to take her to a lama, leaving after dark since religious activities were forbidden. They visited the home of a lama called Jampa Tenzin (byams pa bstan 'dzin), formerly of Ru Gonsar (ru dgon gsar), which was near her former nunnery. Apparently suspecting she was possessed by a deity, Jampa Tenzin performed a tsagoche rite (rtsa sgo phye), literally ""opening the door of the channels,"" a type of purification ritual that readies a person's body to accept the presence of a deity and serve as a medium. After this it appears that her condition began to improve. This is consistent with the well-established phenomenon of religious figures experiencing episodes of madness; these were sometimes understood as part of their path toward enlightenment or attainment of prophetic abilities.[3]

From this point on Trinle Chodron began to enter into trances. Despite a ban on religious activities in Tibet, she frequently became entranced and burned incense, apparently without any consequences from authorities. Her younger brother indicated that her purported mental instability led people to disregard her behavior.

Beginning in early 1967, two factions in Nyemo vied for control of the Tibetan Communist Party structure, each claiming to be the group that could properly institute Mao's visions for reform. These were known as the Nyamdrel (mnyam sbrel), or ""alliance,"" and the Gyenlok (gyen log), or ""over-throw [the powerholders].""[4] Similar infighting led to chaos in many Tibetan regions and culminated in an order from Mao to curtail the activities of counter-revolutionary groups. The Nyamdrel emerged as the more popular group, with far more members throughout Tibetan regions, but in Nyemo, the Gyenlok increasingly gained support from people who opposed the implementation of economic reforms such as collection of sales taxes and mandatory grain donations, as both policies were blamed for food shortages.[5]

Trinle Chodron petitioned to join Gyenlok, likely due to the common local distrust of the cadres in charge of reforms. Her membership in Gyenlok was initially opposed on the grounds of her well-known mental instability, but she was eventually allowed in around the spring of 1968. Once part of the Gyenlok, Trinle Chodron joined in the efforts to destabilize the Nyamdrel faction in Nyemo.

Meanwhile, Trinle Chodron's reputation as a medium increased to the point that people from surrounding villages began to seek her out for healing and prophecies, which became highly regarded for their accuracy. Although Trinle Chodron was reportedly possessed by different deities at various times, she began to be primarily associated with the mythic figure of Ane Gongme Gyelmo (a ne gong smad rgyal mo) also known as Manene Gyelmo (ma ne ne rgyal mo), the aunt of Gesar of Ling (gling ge sar) who guides and protects that legendary hero of Tibetan myth.

Trinle Chodron's position as a medium coexisted with her belief in Mao as an emanation of Mañjuśrī, seeing her role as a spiritual complement to Mao's efforts to address the material concerns of people. Thus, she was effectively able to merge her religious beliefs with aspects of Communist ideology. According to Goldstein, Jiao, and Lhundrup, this was particularly useful for the Gyenlok leadership, which purposefully used Trinle Chodron's popularity to garner support for their anti-Nyamdrel actions.[6]

Two local Gyenlok leaders, Zhang Yongfu, a Han cadre living in Nyemo, and Rangjung (rang byung), a Tibetan cadre who had been born a tseyok on a Shatra (bshad sgra) estate, were then intent on opposing Nyamdrel activities. After disrupting a meeting on grain collection in October of 1968, the two leaders planned further offensives. Rangjung proposed having Trinle Chodron enter a trance to engage local people from Angang, a nearby district, to support an attack on the county seat.

On November 26 hundreds of people from Angang arrived in Pusum Village, but were not easily convinced to attack the Nyemo county seat headquarters. At Rangjung's request, Trinle Chodron entered a trance and channeled Ani Gongme Gyelmo. According to witness accounts, she urged the people to attack the county seat, specifically the enemy cadres of Nyamdrel, assuring them that there would be no casualties because they would have the protection of the deity. She also gave out barley that had been blessed by Lama Jampa Tenzin. By the next day, hundreds of people arrived at the county seat and began to attack and struggle with Nyamdrel cadres in what Goldstein, Jian, and Lhundrup call a ""stunning victory.""[7] Spurred on by their success, in January 1969 Gyenlok leaders met to discuss future plans and the group's organization. It appears that many people, including Rangjung, attributed their success to Trinle Chodron's supernatural powers, viewing her as a protective force in their battle for Gyenlok supremacy, which was eventually named ""Gyenlok Army of the Gods"" (gyen log lha mag). Goldstein et al. note that ""Army for Defending Buddhism"" (bstan srung mag) was also floated but was not well-received.[8]

Goldstein, Jiao, and Lhundrup present Trinle Chodron's possessions and prophecies as an example of the ""Gesar Hysteria"" that pervaded Tibet during the Cultural Revolution, as well as efforts to infuse Mao idolatry with Buddhist imagery. She was one of many who claimed possession by figures from the Gesar legend. While Rangjung and Zhang Yongfu's goals appear to have been oriented toward elevating the Gyenlok faction, others who employed Gesar seemed to have done so out of a desire to ""destroy the enemies of Buddhism.""[9] Eight individuals who also channeled deities were known to regularly stay with Trinle Chodron.

On May 5, 1969, Trinle Chodron entered into trance and delivered a statement that was recorded by the former chant-master of a monastery named Tsering Chozang (tshe ring chos bzang). Although widely reported as incoherent—the Tibetan statement is no longer extant though a Chinese rendering exists—it was clear in its call to action against the People's Liberation Army (PLA) and its reliance on a certainty that Gesar deities would right the perceived political and economic wrongs. Goldstein, Jiao, and Lhundrup surmise that Rangjung instructed Trinle Chodron to make the statement, which was copied ten times and distributed.[10]

On June 3, 1969, a villager named Lhawang Yeshe (lha dbang ye shes) who had previously questioned Trinle Chodron's authority, paid her a visit. His purpose is uncertain; it may have been to voice a newfound faith, or to confess his involvement in the murder and robbery of a lama during the 1959 uprising, or perhaps both.[11] After entering a trance, she is said to have instructed her followers to murder Lhawang Yeshe for his crime. What followed were several weeks of attacks on supposed enemies, resulting in the maiming and death of between fifteen and twenty people in Pusum village. Some of the victims had questioned Trinle Chodron's authenticity as a medium while others were cadres opposed to the Gyenlok faction. Personal enmity was also a factor, as some of the victims had been involved in the ransacking of the Trinle Chodron's family home during earlier class struggles. On June 13, 1969, the Gyenlok militia, led by Rangjung, attacked a government building in the Drakgo (brag sgo) district. Those inside were completely unprepared for the attack and twenty-two people were killed; the Gyenlok army suffered no deaths or injuries.

A day later, Trinle Chodron was visited by some of the attackers who wished to pay their respects and seek further guidance. She assured her followers that they were invincible and would succeed in further actions. However, a subsequent attack at Nyemo government headquarters was met with armed PLA resistance and resulted in dozens of dead and wounded among the Gyenlok forces.

As a result of the disaster some appear to have lost faith while others, led by Rangjung and encouraged by Trinle Chodron's continuing prophecies, waited in the vicinity of Pusum for the inevitable arrival of the PLA, which occurred on June 19th 1969, which they believed they would succeed in repelling. Easily overpowered, Trinle Chodron, Rangjung and others fled into the mountains. Trinle Chodron hid in a cave and was captured by PLA forces around June 21. Once captured, Trine Chodron is said to have not spoken until asking to be allowed to relieve herself. Although she was shackled she nevertheless began to walk along a river away from her captors. A soldier involved in her capture recalled that she nearly managed to escape to the nearby town where she would have been difficult to locate. She was then taken to Lhasa and in early 1970, in front of thousands of people, Trinle Chodron's crimes were listed along with an order for her execution, which was carried out on that same day.[12]

Labeled by the Chinese government an armed counter-revolutionary revolt and counter-revolutionary incident, the Nyemo revolt has also been examined as a nationalist movement, with Trinle Chodron herself called a ""Tibetan Joan of Arc.""[13]  Melvyn Goldstein, Ben Jiao and Tanzen Lhundrup, however, maintain that the conflict was primarily factional and not one of Tibetans rebelling against the Chinese.[14]

Of these events, Tsering Shakya writes, ""The Revolt of 1969 was inspired by the Tibetan's desire to regain some measure of social, psychological, and cultural freedom. It was not, however, a conscious nationalistic uprising, but a cultural response to the chaos of the Cultural revolution.""[15] Writer Jamyang Norbu has written that ""this uprising captured the imagination of the Tibetan people not only because the leader of the Nyemo Rebel faction was a young woman, and a nun at that, but as she transformed Mao’s supreme political campaign into a patriotic religious war against Communist Chinese rule.""[16] In Forbidden Memory, which includes powerful photographs of the aftermath of the Nyemo events, poet and author Tsering Woeser states, ""The events in Nyemo and Pelbar were the bloodiest and most murderous incidents in the Tibetan chapter of the Cultural Revolution, and those about which the most questions remain unanswered.""[17]

Samten Gyatso was a maternal uncle and the main teacher of Tulku Urgyen. He was one of the main compilers and propagators of the revelations of Chokgyur Lingpa, his maternal grandfather. He transmitted the revelations to the Fifteenth Karmapa, and was briefly a tutor to the Sixteenth Karmapa.

","

Samten Gyatso (bsam gtan rgya mtsho) was born around the middle of the nineteenth century in Nangchen, Kham. His father, Orgyen Chopel (o rgyan chos 'phel) was from the Tsangsar family (gtsang sar), a noble house of Nangchen. His mother was Konchok Peldron (dkon mchog dpal sgron, died 1930s), the daughter of the great nineteenth-century treasure revealer Chokgyur Lingpa (mchog 'gyur gling pa, 1829–1870). Like himself, his three brothers all became prominent lamas and lineage holders of Chokgyur Lingpa's revelations: Lama Sangngak (bla ma sangs sngags, d. 1949), Tersey Tulku (gter sras sprul sku, d. 1956), and Chime Dorje ('chi med rdo rje, d. 1948), the father of Tulku Urgyen Karma Orgyen Tsewang Chokdrub Pelbar (sprul sku o rgyan karma o rgyan tshe dbang mchog grub dpal 'bar, 1920–1996). He and his brothers spent much of their youth at Tsangsar Lhalam Monastery (gtsang sar lha lam dgon), the family monastery of his father.

Samten Gyatso was identified as the third reincarnation of Ngawang Trinle (ngag dbang 'phrin las), a patriarch of the Tsangsar clan, and was enthroned as the Fourth Ngatrin Tulku (ngag 'phrin sprul sku) at the seat of his incarnation line, Lachab Monastery (bla khyab dgon).[1] Like Lhalam, Lachab was traditionally a Barom Kagyu monastery, controlled by the Tsangsar family, which, due to the influence of Konchok Peldron and her children, was a center for the practice of the revelations of Chokgyur Lingpa. Samten Gyatso's teacher there was a lama named Chowang Tulku (chos dbang sprul sku), who was said to have been the reincarnation of Guru Chowang (gu ru chos dbang, 1212–1270).[2] He was also a disciple of Karmey Khenpo (kar ma'i mkhen po, c.1860–c.1939),[3] who was a close disciple of Chokgyur Lingpa. Karmey Khenpo gave Sonam Gyatso his monastic ordination. A third master was his maternal uncle, Chokgyur Lingpa's son Tsewang Norbu (tshe dbang nor bu, d. 1856).[4]

He spent his youth at Lachab and its hermitage, Dzonggo Ling (rdzong mgo gling) before moving to Tsike Monastery (rtsi ke dgon), one of two centers established by Chokgyur Lingpa and the seat of the Second Kela Chokling, Konchok Gyurme (ke la mchog gling 02 dkon mchog 'gyur med, 1871–1939) also known as Tsike Chokling (rtsi ke mchog gling).[5]He went there to study with Karmey Khenpo, who shared the administration of the monastery with the Kela Chokling.[6]

Samten Gyatso is said to have strictly observed the monastic codes, never taking alcohol or meat, and was meticulous in his ritual performances.[7] Tulku Urgyen describes him as intimidating, even to high lamas such as the Sixteenth Karmapa Rangjung Rigpai Dorje (karma pa 16 rang byung rig pa'i rdo rje, 1924-1981).[8] He was stern and without pretense, refusing to allow people wear elaborate robes or to prostrate to him.[9]

Samten Gyatso was one of the main compilers and propagators of the New Revelations of Chokgyur Lingpa, which was initially printed in nine volumes by the Second Kela Chokling. Tulku Urgyen describes how his uncle would travel with scribes to copy out any of the treasure texts he came across, dedicating himself to collecting and preserving the handwritten manuscripts. The collecting also involved receiving the transmission, which largely came from either Tsewang Norbu or Karmey Khenpo. His search for scripture was not restricted to the revelations of Chokgyur Lingpa; he would apparently unwrap any text in a home or temple that he came across to examine it.[10] Samten Gyatso also requested the Fifteenth Karmapa, Khakyab Dorje (karma pa 15 bka' khyab rdo rje, 1870–1922) to compose needed liturgies for the collection[11]—the Fourteenth Karmapa, Tekchok Dorje (karma pa 14 theg mchog rdo rje, 1798–1868) had been a close collaborator with Chokgyur Lingpa in many of the revelations. Samten Gyatso's extensive library was destroyed during the Cultural Revolution.

This life-long endeavor, according to Tulku Urgyen, was inspired by an order from Tsewang Norbu. While Samten Gyatso was a young man he received the transmission of Jamgon Kongtrul's ('jam mgon kong sprul, 1813­–1899) Treasury of Revelations at Riwoche Monastery (ri bo che dgon), given by Tsewang Norbu. During the months-long transmission Tsewang Norbu singled Samten Gyatso out in a room full of lamas, calling him the ""pillar upholding the teachings of Chokgyur Lingpa.""[12] Soon after, Tsewang Norbu passed through the Tsangsar home on his way to central Tibet and called Samten Gyatso into his large tent. There he insisted Samten Gyatso accept empowerment as a holder of the teachings, giving him a number of his own ritual implements and a set of his own robes.

Samten Gyatso gathered multiple transmissions of the New Revelations where possible. For example, he held two distinct lineages of the important Three Sections of Dzogchen. He had received this from Tsewang Norbu as part of the complete transmission, but he sought out a second transmission from his younger brother, Lama Sangngak. Soon after Chokgyur Lingpa passed away he appeared to Karmey Khenpo in a vision to bestow the Three Sections of Dzogchen, which Karmey Khenpo had failed to receive while the master was alive. Karmey Khenpo passed this distinct transmission only to Lama Sangngak.[13] According to Tulku Urgyen, this treasure cycle was restricted for three generations, only becoming available for public transmission with Tulku Urgyen himself.[14]

While still a young man, Samten Gyatso accompanied his mother to Tsurpu (mtshur phu) to transmit the New Revelations of Chokgyur Lingpa to the Fifteenth Karmapa. The Karmapa had apparently been unsuccessful in convincing Tsewang Norbu to give him the transmission, and thus turned to Samten Gyatso. Like Tsewang Norbu had done, the Karmapa insisted on enthroning Samten Gyatso as a holder of the teachings, additionally demanding that he forsake his desire to live in isolated caves and instead serve as a lama, performing public empowerments and teachings, much to Samten Gyatso's dismay.[15]

Around the year 1920 or 1921 Samten Gyatso's brother Chime Dorje and his family were staying at Sangngak Choling (gsang sngags chos gling), the seat of the Tenth Drukchen, Mipam Chokyi Wangpo (mi 'pham chos kyi dbang po, 1884–1930), a teacher of Chime Dorje and his brothers. Samten Gyatso was at Tsurpu Monastery transmitting the complete revelations, known as the New Treasures of Chokgyur Lingpa (mchog gling gter gsar) to the Fifteenth Karmapa. Chime Dorje wrote to his brother asking him to request a name for his newborn son from the Karmapa. Samten Gyatso sent the Karmapa's reply, a name written in the Karmapa's own hand, along with the pronouncement that the child, Tulku Urgyen, was a ""genuine tulku.""[16]

He later took up the leadership of Lachab Monastery.[17] At Lachab Samten Gyatso formally enthroned Tulku Urgyen as the reincarnation of his own root teacher, Chowang Tulku, an identity that was determined by the young Sixteenth Karmapa, Rigpai Dorje.[18]

In the late 1930s the leadership of Karma Gon (karma dgon) appointed Samten Gyatso the tutor of the young Sixteenth Karmapa, who was then arriving in Kham from Tsurpu. The Karmapa's previous tutor, Ninth Gangkar Lama, Karma Shedrub Chokyi Sengge (gangs dkar bla ma 09 karma bshad sgrub chos kyi seng+ge, 1892–1957), who was considered one of the finest Karma Kagyu scholars of his generation, had been dismissed for not being sufficiently deferential to the Karmapa. The Karmapa was apparently not a diligent student, and the famous lama did not shy away from traditional forms of discipline, including pinching and even striking the Karmapa.[19] According to Tulku Urgyen, Samten Gyatso never beat the Karmapa; instead, when the teenage lama misbehaved, his tutor would strike his own attendant, a lama named Dudul (bdud 'dul), which would quickly convince the compassionate Karmapa to sit and focus on his studies.[20] The elderly Samten Gyatso held the position only briefly, receiving permission to step down when the Karmapa arrived at Pelpung Monastery (dpal spungs).[21]

Around the year 1938 Samten Gyatso gave the transmission of the New Revelations of Chokgyur Lingpa at Zurmang Dutsitil (zur mang bdud rtsi dil). This was sponsored by the Tenth Zurmang Tentrul, Karma Lodro Gyatso Drayang (zur mang bstan sprul 10 karma blo gros rgya mtsho'i sgra dbyangs). Samten Gyatso and his brother Chime Dorje presided over the three-month ceremony; Samten Gyatso gave the empowerments and Chime Dorje the reading transmission. Near the end of the three months Samten Gyatso is said to have informed Tentrul that additional transmissions would be given to only select advanced students, and that Tentrul would have the duty of deciding who might receive them.

According to Tulku Urgyen, who initially served as a shrine attendant but then was permitted to sit and receive the transmissions, despite announcing that only lamas and ordained monks would receive the restricted empowerments, several dozen members of the Nangchen nobility sat behind a curtain intent on receiving them. Because of their presence Samten Gyatso angrily refused to continue, and instructed his attendants to pack his things. Chime Dorje and Karmey Khentrul both intervened on the behalf of the terrified Zurmang Tentrul, who was bearing the brunt of Samten Gyatso displeasure. Samten Gyatso continued the empowerments only after several days of offering ceremonies to repair the breach of samaya.[22] Even so, he held back the Three Sections of Dzogchen, which was not yet deemed appropriate to transmit publicly.[23]

Among his disciples were the Second Kela Chokling, Konchok Gyurme, who was older than him and the king of Nangchen, Tashi Tsewang Tobyal (bkras shis tshe dbang stobs rgyal). Samten Gyatso's mother regarded him as her root guru and received from him pointing out instructions and meditation instructions.[24] Samten Gyatso's younger brother Sangngak was also a disciple, and lived with him for several years as an attendant. It was around this time that Lama Sangngak urged Tulku Urgyen to ordain, with the Second Jamgon Kongtrul, Khyentse Wozer ('jam mgon kon sprul 02 mkhyen brtse 'od zer, 1904–1953) as preceptor, offering him all his possessions were he to do so. Samten Gyatso, remained silent on the matter.[25]

In his memoir, Tulku Urgyen praises Samten Gyatso highly, noting that he was considered both an emanation of Four-Armed Mahākāla and, according to a vision of the Second Tsike Chokling, of Vimalamitra. Although Samten Gyatso would not allow others to speak of his accomplishments, insisting that he had none, one evening, speaking from his bed to Tulku Urgyen, who was lying on the floor, he stated that he had realized the nature of mind at the age of eight and had, despite distraction, maintained the awareness.[26]

According to Tulku Urgyen, several months before Samten Gyatso passed away he had presided over a drubchen (sgrub chen) ceremony with his three brothers. Chime Dorje reported that over the course of three days Samten Gyatso's body glowed with increasingly intense rainbow light, a sight witnessed by the other two brothers as well. Intimidated by their brother to the very end of his life, none of them had the courage to speak to him about it.[27]

His main practices were Chokgyur Lingpa's revelation Kunzang Tuktik (kun bzang thugs thig), or Heart Essence of Samantabhadra and Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo's revelation Chetsun Nyintik (lce btsun snying thig). The first is a practice on the peaceful and wrathful deities, while the second is considered one of Khyentse's most important Dzogchen revelations.  Tulku Urgyen also states that his two most valued scriptures were The Seed Tantra that is the Only Child of All Buddhas (sangs rgyas thams cad kyi sras gcig gsang ba cod pan sa bon gyi rgyud) and Chokgyur Lingpa's Lotus Essence Tantra (padma snying po rgyud).

Samten Gyatso passed away in the late 1930s or 1940 at Tsurpu. His reincarnation is Tsewang Dechen, who was born in 1941 and recognized by the Sixteenth Karmapa in 1950 and enthroned at Lachab, where he lived until 1958 when he was forced to leave by the new Communist government. In 1980 he began rebuilding Lachab and Dzonggo Ling, which were destroyed during the Cultural Revolution.

The Third Belmang was a Geluk lama based at Labrang Monastery in Amdo. He served as abbot of Amchok and Shitsang monasteries as well as two monastic colleges at Labrang.

","

The Third Belmang, Jamyang Tenzin Gyatso (dbal mang 03 'jam dbyangs bstan 'dzin rgya mtsho, 1854–1919) was born on February 17, 1854 in Chokhor Shitsang (chos 'khor shis tshang), Amdo. His father, Konchok Kyab (dkon mchog skyabs), was the chieftain (dpon) of Chokhor Shitsang, which comprised of the ""Twelve Chokhor Communities"" (chos 'khor tsho ba bcu gnyis) and is currently administered under Luchu Dzong (klu cho rdzong). His mother was named Tsering Kyi (tshe ring skyid). The local astrologer, who the family invited to chart a natal horoscope, named the child Lama Tsering (bla ma tshe ring).

A few years had passed since the demise of the Second Belmang, Konchok Gyeltsen (dbal mang 02 dkon mchog rgyal mtshan, 1764–1853) and the search for the reincarnation by high lamas and local monasteries was underway. The Third Detri Rinpoche, Jamyang Tubten Nyima (sde khri 03 'jam dbyangs thub bstan nyi ma, 1779–1862), received a list of child candidates on July 20, 1858, which coincided with Chokhor Duchen (chos 'khor dus chen), the holiday celebrating the Buddha's first teaching, i.e., ""first turning of the wheel of dharma. The Third Detri was at the time the head of Labrang Tashikhyil (bla brang bkra shis 'khyil), the seat of the Belmang incarnations. After performing lamp divinations (sgron me'i brtag pa) through the night, he identified the young child Lama Tsering as the reincarnation of the Second Belmang Rinpoche the following day.

As the Second Belmang had taught extensively at the nearby Amchok Monastery (a mchog dga' ldan chos 'khor gling dgon), upon hearing the news of the discovery hundreds of people from Amchok and neighboring regions traveled to the birthplace and set up tent camps for celebration. There, representatives of high lamas and the abbot of Amchok Monastery extended gifts such as monastic robes. Locals, including disciples of Second Belmang, made offerings and sought his blessings. The abbot of Amchok, Sera Ponlob Lobzang Nyima (se ra dpon slob blo bzang nyi ma, d. circa 1890) held an enthronement ceremony in his honor. The young incarnation was then invited to the monasteries of Chone Gon (co ne dgon) and Dzoge Garsar (mdzo dge sgar gsar).

Then on September 29, 1858, the young reincarnate arrived at Labrang Tashikhyil where he was received by the Third Detri Rinpoche, the Fourth Hortsang Sertri Jigme Tenpai Nyima (hor tshang gser khri 04 'jigs med bstan pa'i nyi ma, b. 1816), and the Fourth Gungtang, Konchok Tenpai Gyatso (gung thang 04 dkon mchog bstan pa'i rgya mtsho, 1824–1859).

In 1859, at the age of six, the Third Detri gave the young Belmang Tulku the layperson's vows (dge bsnyen gyi sdom pa), followed by the probationary monastic vows (bar ma rab byung gi sdom pa), and bestowed upon him the ordination name of Jamyang Tenzin Gyatso. He also gifted his well-used square-mat (gding ba) to ensure the young lama a successful monastic life. Amchok Chojor Gyatso (a mchog chos 'byor rgya mtsho), who was a disciple of the former Belmang Rinpoche, was assigned to serve as his personal tutor. The young incarnate began his training in monastic chants and rituals, the fundamentals of language and grammar, and other fields of religious and philosophical studies.

In the spring of 1864, the young Belmang Rinpoche formally joined Labrang Monastery. There he began his formal monastic training, starting from the fundamentals of dialectics, logic, and epistemology. Like other novice monks, he memorized the monastery chants and prayers.

After his basic training, he began his advanced training in the five traditional fields—logic, soteriology, metaphysics, philosophy, and ethics. At the same time, he received tantric initiations, transmissions, and instructions (dbang lung man ngag) from multiple lamas. The Third Detri conferred an oral transmission of all his own writings, which were already compiled in six-volumes. The Third Tranye, Ngawang Tubten Gyatso (pra nye 03 ngag dbang thub bstan rgya mtsho, 1836–1869), who was a disciple of his previous incarnation, gave him the transmission of the collected works of Je Tsongkhapa (tsong kha pa blo bzang grags pa, 1357-1419) and those of his two disciples, as well as the collected works of the Third Changkya Rolpai Dorje (lcang skya 03 rol pa'i rdo rje, 1717–1786), the Second Jamyang Zhepa Konchok Jigme Wangpo ('jam dbyangs bzhad pa 02 dkon mchog 'jigs med dbang po, 1728–1791), and the Third Gungtang Konchok Tenpai Dronme (gung thang 03 dkon mchog bstan pa'i sgron me, 1762–1823).

The Third Tranye also gave him the transmission of the collected works of his predecessor, the Second Belmang, which contain more than eight volumes of writings on multiple traditional fields and topics. The Second Belmang's History of India, Tibet and Mongolia (rgya bod hor sog gi lo rgyus), for example, not only provides historical facts on Tibet, India, China, and Mongolia but also contains information on Tibetan-Mongol relations on the Tibetan frontier. This prepared the young Third Belmang for a life of diplomacy between the three main powers of the region. Hortsang Rinpoche gave him the transmission of the collected works of Lhodrak Namkha Gyaltsen (lho brag nam mkha' rgyal mtshan, 1326–1401). After nearly two decades of training, young Belmang Rinpoche not only grew into a monastic scholar, but became a holder of multiple textual transmissions.
In the mid-1870s, he received his bhikṣu (dge slong) ordination at Labrang Monastery. He continued his training in the traditional fields of religious and philosophical studies for nearly a decade.

He then served as the throne-holder of the general assembly (tshogs chen khri pa) and consecutively as abbot of Gyume Dratsang (rgyud smad grwa tshang) as well as Kyedor Dratsang (kyai rdor grwa tshang), which was then newly founded in 1879 by the Fourth Jamyang Zhepa, Kelzang Tubten Wangchuk ('jam dbyangs bzhad pa 04 skal bzang thub bstan dbang phyug, 1856–1916).

He later became the abbot of Amchok Monastery and Shitsang Gonsar (shis tshang dgon gsar). In 1894, the Fourth Jamyang Zhepa appointed him the sikyong (srid skyong), or chief administrator, of Shitsang Gongsar. He was offered a palanquin, a canopy, and other official items. He was also honored with the title of sertri (gser khri), meaning ""[the holder of] the golden throne."" After assuming the position, he lived in Shitsang Gonsar and oversaw its administration and religious education and practice for over two decades.

Later, when Jamyang Zhepa died in 1916, he left a will appointing the Third Belmang as his gyeltsab (rgyal tshab), i.e., regent. Belmang then moved to Labrang Monastery and appointed Li Tsondru (lis brtson 'grus) as the chandzo (phyag mdzod), or treasurer, of Labrang Monastery. Li secretly communicated with the Hui warlord brothers then based in Xining (zi ling), Ma Bufang (1903–1975) and Ma Buqing (1901–1977), who were plotting to gain greater control over the region. When locals discovered the collusion, Li Tsondru fled to the Hui warlords, and in the ensuing years the warlords attacked Labrang Monastery as well as other lay and monastic communities. Belmang fled to Ngulra (rngul ra) in Gyarong.

Although the Tibetans fought against the Ma forces, they were defeated. The Ma forces ransacked Labrang Monastery and its communities. They also looted and destroyed over thirty monasteries, including Amchok Monastery, where they razed the assembly halls of the three monastic colleges, a library that served as repository of thousands of xylographic blocks, and some two hundred monastic quarters built over more than a hundred years.

The Third Belmang died in Ngulra on the thirteenth day of the seventh month of Tibetan Earth-Sheep Year, September 8, 1919, at the age of sixty-five. The monks of Shitsang and Amchok conducted funerary rites and built a stūpa at the cremation site. Before his death, he was said to have summoned his aides and disciples and gave them the letter in which the Fourth Jamyang Zhepa appointed him to his administrative positions, asking them to keep it safe until his return. A few years later, Jigme Tsultrim Namgyel (dbal mang 04 'jigs med tshul khrims rnam rgyal, 1918/20–1957), the younger brother of the Fifth Jamyang Zhepa Yeshe Tenpai Gyaltsen ('jam dbyangs bzhad pa 05 ye shes bstan pa'i rgyal mtshan, 1916–1947), was identified as his reincarnation.

The Fourth Belmang was a Geluk lama based at Labrang Monastery in the early twentieth century. His elder brother was the Fifth Zhamyang Zhepa, and his family used their status to gather power and influence in the region.

","

The Fourth Belmang, Jigme Tsultrim Namgyel (dbal mang 04 'jigs med tshul khrims rnam rgyal), was born in either 1918 or 1920 in Tsema Drong (mtshe ma grong) village of Litang, Kham. His father was Gonpo Dondrub (mgon po don grub) of the Ga Lari (lga bla ri) family, and his mother was Guru Lhatso (gu ru lha mtsho). His two elder brothers were Apa Alo Lobzang Tsewang (a pa a blo blo bzang tshe dbang, 1903–1997) and the Fifth Jamyang Zhepa Yeshe Tenpai Gyeltsen ('jam dbyangs bzhad pa 05 ye shes bstan pa'i rgyal mtshan, 1916–1947). Two elder sisters, Adrol (a sgrol), and Aso (a bsod), married into the Golok chieftain families of Khangsar Pon (khang gsar dpon) and Khanggen Pon (khang rgan dpon), respectively.

Both Tibetan and Western scholars and biographers have proposed 1918 as his year of birth, suggesting that the young reincarnate was born before the death of his predecessor, the Third Belmang, Jamyang Tenzin Gyatso (dbal mang 03 'jam dbyangs bstan 'dzin rgya mtsho, 1854–1919), an obvious contravention of the logic of reincarnation.[1] Such deviations from the otherwise linear progression of the rebirth process based on the law of causality are not unprecedented in Tibetan Buddhist communities. Categories such as a ""pre-death reincarnation (ma 'das sprul sku) and ""supreme nirmāṇakāya"" (mchog gi sprul sku) exist to account for such eventualities, although neither appear to have been employed in this situation, and the birth date of 1920 is also proposed as an alternative.

Before the Third Belmang died in Ngulra (rngul rwa) on the thirteenth day of the seventh month of Tibetan Earth-Sheep Year, i.e., September 8, 1919, he allegedly expressed a desire to be reborn as a sibling of Tamdrin Wanggyel (rta mgrin dbang rgyal), which is the given name of the Fifth Jamyang Zhepa. If Belmang had in fact made such a statement, then he knew the Fifth Jamyang Zhepa as a child before his recognition by the Ninth Paṇchen Lama a year after the Third Belmang died. This narrative is used to confirm that the Fourth Belmang was not conceived before September 1919, i.e., the year the Third Belmang died.

Locals also maintain that the Fourth Jamyang Zhepa, Kelzang Tubten Wangchuk ('jam dbyangs bzhad pa 04 skal bzang thub bstan dbang phyug, 1856–1916) had once expressed his desire to be born as a sibling to a future Belmang reincarnation, and even exclaimed that the two would make ""a formidable pair!""

In 1924, when the Ninth Paṇchen Lama, Tubten Chokyi Nyima (paN chen 09 thub bstan chos kyi nyi ma, 1883–1937), visited Lanju Khar (lan ju mkhar), the young Fifth Jamyang Zhepa and his brother had an audience. Following a request from the monastic and lay parishioners of Amchok (a mchog dgon) and Shitsang Gonsar (shis tshang dgon gsar), the Ninth Paṇchen Lama recognized the young Jamyang Zhepa's brother as the Fourth Belmang reincarnation.

The Fourth Belmang joined Labrang Tashikhyil Monastery (bla brang bkra shis 'khyil) in 1927. Drakpa Taye (grags pa mtha' yas), a resident scholar who earlier had served as tutor to the Seventh Tukwan Kelzang Chokyi Nyima (thu'u bkwan 07 skal bzang dam chos nyi ma, 1895/1898–1959), became the Fourth Belmang’s tutor and taught him reading, writing, and chanting of monastery prayers. At around this time, the Fourth Belmang received the probationary monastic vows (bar ma rab byung gi sdom pa) from Lakho Jigme Trinle Gyatso (bla kho 'jigs med 'phrin las rgya mtsho, 1866–1948), who also gave him the monastic name Jigme Tsultrim Namgyel ('jigs med tshul khrims rnam rgyal).
In 1928, the young Belmang joined Tosam Norling Dratsang (thos bsam nor gling grwa tshang), the college for philosophical studies at Labrang Monastery.

There, he pursued advanced education and training in what are known as the five major treatises (gzhung chen dka' pod lnga)—Guṇaprabha's Vinayasūtra, or Fundamentals of Discipline ('dul ba mdo rtsa), Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośa, or Treasury on Metaphysics (chos mngon pa mdzod), Candrakīrti's Madhamikāvatāra, or Supplement to the Middle Way (dbu ma 'jug pa), Maitreyanatha's Abhisamayālaṃkāra, or Ornament of Clear Realization (sher phyin mngon rtogs rgyan), and Dharmakīrti's Pramāṇavārttika, or Commentary to Valid Cognition (tshad ma rnam 'grel). He completed his first major exam on this last topic in 1936.
He excelled in his class, which had about a dozen reincarnate lamas and nearly 200 students. From a young age, he was assigned the task of monitoring and mentoring fellow students.

In the meantime, Belmang's father and brother Apa Alo were gathering power and influence in the Amdo area by virtue of being the family members of the Jamyang Zhepa, whose jurisdiction extended over the monasteries of Labrang, Amchok, and Shitsang Gonsar, as well as hundreds of farming and nomadic communities in Amdo. While the reincarnations of Jamyang Zhepa received and used the official seals of authority granted by the traditional Tibetan government in central Tibet, the family enjoyed considerable political and military clout in the region by establishing new affiliations with neighboring Chinese warlords and Hui Muslims leaders. They also granted permission to Christian missionaries to run a missionary station in the area.

In 1936, the Fourth Belmang met the Ninth Paṇchen Lama during his visit to Labrang Monastery, where the latter conferred a Kālacakra initiation. Belmang Rinpoche, like his predecessors, received the transmission of the Paṇchen lineage. During these years, Belmang also sought teachings and transmissions from various masters.

Belmang traveled to Lhasa with his brother Jamyang Zhepa in 1937 and visited the main Gelukpa monasteries in the region. Both brothers enrolled at Gomang College (sgo mang grwa tshang) of Drepung Monastery ('bras spung dgon), where the renowned master Khangsar Ngawang Tubten Chokyi Wangchuk (khang gsar ngag dbang thub bstan chos kyi dbang phyug, 1888–1941) became their tutor. Belmang undertook an advanced study of the Abhisamayālaṃkāra and visited other monasteries in central Tibet, including Sakya Monastery (sa skya dgon), where he received Lamdre and Hevajra teachings from Sakya Dakchen Kunga Rinchen (sa skya bdag chen kun dga' rin chen, 1902–1950).

He and his brother returned to Labrang Monastery in 1940. His brother was said to have founded Labrang Gyuto Dratsang in 1928 to complement the Gyume Dratsang at Labrang Monastery, founded by the First Jamyang Zhepa ('jam dbyangs bzhad pa, 1648-1721/1722). Together, these colleges replicate the two Lhasa tantric monasteries of Gyuto (rgyud stod grwa tshang) and Gyume (rgyud stod grwa tshang). Like the First Jamyang Zhepa, the Fifth Jamyang Zhepa brought along Gyuto tantric masters from Lhasa. As instructed by his brother, Belmang Rinpoche oversaw the fundraising and construction of infrastructure, including a twenty-four-columned assembly hall, a three-storied protector chapel, and a ritual courtyard. In 1943, Belmang Rinpoche and his brother, the Fifth Jamyang Zhepa, were able to inaugurate the college, which formally came to be known as Gyuto Sangchen Dorje Ling (rgyud stod gsang chen rdo rje gling).

In 1945, the Fifth Jamyang Zhepa's influential treasurer (mdzod pa) Choje Khyenrab Dondrub (chos rje mkhyen rab don grub) suddenly fell ill. Belmang Rinpoche brought Choje to his residence and personally nursed him, but was unable to save his life. Khyenrab Dondrub was one of the most influential persons at Labrang Monastery, because he formed an alliance of parishioners and neighboring communities to defend against external intruders and warlords for more than two decades. After his death, Belmang Rinpoche succeeded him and assumed religious and administrative responsibilities at the behest of his brother, the Fifth Jamyang Zhepa.

From 1945, with his newfound position, Belmang Rinpoche went on to hold various administrative roles for the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), including founding the Amdo Monthly Journal (Anduo Yuekan 安多月刊). Belmang and his brother would later join the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), which would see the elevation of his brother Apa Alo as the Governor of the Gannan Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture. Belmang was involved in mediating disputes over grasslands between communities in the region.

In 1947, when the Fifth Jamyang Zhepa died, the Fourth Belmang became the regent (rgyal tshab) of Labrang and its affiliated institutions. He maintained peace in the community and extended relations with monasteries of all Tibetan Buddhist traditions. He supervised the search for the incarnation of his late brother, consulting the Tenth Paṇchen Lama, Lobzang Chokyi Gyaltsen (paN chen 10 blo bzang chos kyi rgyal mtshan, 1938–1989).

Following the recognition of the Sixth Jamyang Zhepa, Jigme Tubten Chokyi Nyima ('jam dbyangs bzhad pa 06, b.1948), by the Teṇth Panchen Lama, Belmang Rinpoche escorted the young reincarnation and his family to Labrang Monastery and conducted the enthronement ceremony, on April 5, 1952. With the family of the young incarnate having now arrived in Labrang, Belmang Rinpoche resigned from his treasury position.

In 1952, in his early 30s, he left for Beijing and studied language, political science, and history at Minzu National University. He returned to Amdo after a year away. He then held leading official positions in the Committee on Governance in the Border Regions of Three Provinces of Qinghai, Gansu, and Sichuan and the Machu County administration. His tenure would coincide with the years when the CCP newly enforced Democratic Reforms in Amdo and Kham were marked by Tibetan resistance.

In the early spring of 1957, Belmang Rinpoche became ill, and his health gradually deteriorated. He was distraught by the CCP's forceful confiscation of monastery land and limitation of power under its Democratic Reform policies. Tibetan and Chinese physicians administered medication and monks conducted religious rituals to attempt to prolong his life. During a particular long-life ceremony, when monastics and lay parishioners supplicated him to live for a long time, he was said to have bluntly asserted, ""I know well when I should go."" Later, when the Sixth Jamyang Zhepa sent monks to offer a long-life supplication, he was said to have pulled a blanket over his head and refused to acknowledge their presence. Similarly, when the representatives from Gyuto and Gyume pleaded with him, he refused to accept their long-life supplications. Finally, he died lying in a traditional ""lion pose"" (seng ge nyal stabs) in the morning hours of the eleventh day of the second Hor lunar month, i.e., April 10, of 1957. Monasteries and lay communities observed extensive post-funerary rituals for his swift return.

The chaos of the Communist takeover of Tibet and the subsequent Cultural Revolution prevented the identification of his reincarnation for several decades. In 1992, the Sixth Jamyang Zhepa, having secured permission from the Chinese government to search and identify reincarnations, performed a divination in the presence of more than a dozen Amdo lamas, as well as the Fourth Belmang's brother Alo Lobzang Tsewang. He identified a fifteen-year old boy named Drolma Tseten (sgrol ma tshe brtan) as the Fifth Belmang, who was given the name Lobzang Pelden Gyatso (dbal mang 05 blo bzang dpal ldan rgya mtsho, b. 1977).
