Dawa Drolma was a twentieth-century delok—someone who travels to the realms beyond death and returns to tell about it. Born into a prominent nomad family in Kham, she was guided through her trip through the afterlife by Tromge Kundun Rinpoche. She was the mother of Chagdud Tulku.

","

Dawa Drolma (zla ba sgrol ma) was born the daughter of Jigme Trogyel ('jigs med khro rgyal), a lama of the Tromge (khrom dge) clan who resided in the Washul Trom (wa shul khrom) region of Kham, also known as Tromtar (khrom thar). Her paternal uncle was a prominent tulku named Drime Kacho Wangpo (dri med mkha' spyod dbang po). Her brother was Tromge Trungpa Rinpoche (khrom dge drungs pa rin po che), and she had another older brother named Pelchen (dpal chen).

According to her autobiography, Delog: Journey to Realms Beyond Death, as translated by Richard Barron, as a toddler she enjoyed being generous to the poor and often gave away items of great value to beggars who showed up at her family's large tent. At a young age, she accumulated many recitations of mantras and prayers, and she claims to have had countless visions of various deities, many of whom shared prophesies with her.

As an adolescent, she experienced a number of inauspicious visions, dreams, and bouts of sickness, suggesting that her life was in danger. To counteract obstacles to her life, her brother Tromge Trungpa and her root guru, Tromge Kundun Sonam Rinchen (khrom dge sku mdun bsod nams rin chen), performed extensive rituals and her health improved.

In her autobiography, she recounts how her uncle Drime Kacho Wangpo guided her through a visionary experience in which she was able to ask deities for advice about her health and future activities. She was instructed to do extensive recitations of the mantras of the long-life deity Amitāyus, Śrī Samyak, and Vajrakīlaya. Drime Kacho Wangpo then initiated her into these practices based on the treasure teachings of Lekyi Dorje (las kyi rdo rje, 1326–1401). After receiving these empowerments, she recounts that she gained profound and stable insight into the true nature of reality.

In 1924, when she was sixteen, she recounted many of her dreams and visions to Tromge Kundun, including a prophecy she received from Tārā predicting that she would, before long, spend about a week in a state of deep sleep, or in a death-like coma. This alarmed Tromge Kundun and Tromge Trungpa, who urged her to avoid entering such a perilous state and to focus on conventional longevity practices, rituals, and animal life-ransoming. Headstrong, she did not follow the advice of her gurus and felt that she could not avoid the experience that Tārā had foretold.

Two days later, at a gaṇacakra feast with her teachers and friends, she announced that she would soon go on her journey beyond the threshold of death. Tromge Kundun, now resigned to her plan, gave her final advice about how to handle herself in the intermediate states, or bardo (bar do).

Dawa Drolma instructed them to lock her in her room and to not disturb the solemnity of the environment. She underwent elaborate preparations and requested that her teachers perform continuous rituals to dispel any problems during her experience. On the evening of the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month, she recounts that she settled into a spacious, nonconceptual state of meditation and her journey began.

Sometime the next morning she had a vivid vision of White Tārā and many of her attendant goddesses. She traveled with them through ethereal realms while experiencing intense and shifting meditative experiences. Eventually, she said that she reached Padmasambhava's divine abode, the Copper-Colored Mountain, where she was granted an audience with the great master and offered him prostrations, confession, and maṇḍala offerings. She remembers that Padmasambhava smiled and was friendly and shared blessed food with her.

Her vision continues with a ḍākinī escorting her into the presence of the great nineteenth-century master Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo ('jam dbyangs mkhyen brtse'i dbang po, 1820–1892), to whom she also extended many gestures of respect and devotion. Interestingly, about this audience, she recalled, ""The lama seemed to have a very harsh and intractable character; he spoke not a single word and deliberately avoided looking at me.""

As her physical body remained as if dead for a full five days, she recalls that her mind continued to journey, meeting countless deities, ḍākinīs, and beings in other realms. She recorded the names of many of the beings she encountered, and it is said that she was later able to convey messages to the relatives they had left behind in the human realm.

Finally, she said that the deity Tashi Tseringma (bkra shis tshe ring ma) directed her to return to the human realm, and she woke up in the presence of Tromge Trungpa. After resting for a few days, she began recounting her adventures, which were written down by Gyazur Tulku (rgya zur sprul sku). This experience earned her the title of delok ('das log), loosly translated as ""one who returns from death.""

Around the following year, Dawa Drolma attended ceremonies led by Chagdud Tenpai Gyeltsen (lcags mdud bstan pa'i rgyal mtshan), the leader of Chagdud Monastery ( lcags mdud dgon). Intrigued by the young woman, Chagdud Rinpoche called her into his presence, offered her a reliquary box, and told her that they would meet again before long. Shortly after, he passed away.[i] This encounter, witnessed by many, was considered strong evidence for the future recognition of her son as the reincarnation of Chagdud Tenpai Gyeltsen.

Dawa Drolma went next to Lhasa on pilgrimage where she had a secret intimate relationship with the important Geluk lama, the Fifth Khardo Tulku Kelzang Tubten Nyendrak (mkhar rdo sprul sku 05 bskal bzang thub bstan snyan grags, 1908–1951), of Sera Monastery (se ra dgon).[ii] Khardo Rinpoche was involved in the Tibetan government as a close friend and associate of the Fifth Reting Rinpoche Jampel Yeshe Gyeltsen (rwa sgreng 05 'jam dpal ye shes rgyal mtshan, 1912–1947), the regent of the Fourteenth Dalai Lama (ta la'i bla ma 14, b, 1935). She conceived a child with Khardo Tulku who was later recognized as the Sixteenth Chagdud Tulku, Pema Gargyi Wangchuk (lcags mdud sprul sku pad+ma gar gyi dbang phyug, 1930–2002). Khardo Rinpoche acknowledged the tulku by letter to Dawa Drolma and even sent a nun from Lhasa to train the child for a brief period. Khardo was imprisoned for his political activity in 1947. He was released after a few years, but he passed away in 1951.

Dawa Drolma lived with her parents in Tromtar until about 1934, when she began a relationship with a Geluk lama named Sodga (bsod dga') who was associated with Bumsar Monastery ('bum gsar dgon) near the larger Tenpel Monastery (bstan 'phel dgon). They relocated near Tenpel Monastery, where she lived as a respected teacher and ḍākinī who was often invited to confer empowerments and conduct rituals. With Sodga, she would give birth to a daughter, Trinle Wangmo ('phrin las dbang mo, b. 1940), who is widely recognized as an advanced practitioner.

In 1941 Dawa Drolma was invited to perform rituals by a powerful Derge minister. Upon their conclusion, she spoke about impermanence and asked the minister and his family to take care of her children if anything happened to her. A few months later, in her mid-thirties, after giving birth to a baby boy, she passed away. The child also passed away two years later.
It is said that her body remained in meditation posture for several days and that during her cremation, vultures circled the fire and rainbows appeared in the sky.

Jangsem Choje Sonam Gyeltsen was a thirteenth-century practitioner of the Aural Lineage of Rechungpa. He was the father of Kunden Rema.

","

Jangsem Choje Sonam Gyeltsen (byang sems chos rje bsod nams rgyal mtshan) was born at the top of the small mountain at Tsongdu Gurmo (tshong 'dus 'gur mo) in eastern Tibet. When he was a baby, his father met with Lama Zhang Lotsawa (bla ma zhang, 1123–1193) and told him that he had a son. The master said, ""That son of yours will subdue enemies and become the leader of a district (yul gru). He will be a great tantric practitioner (sngags pa).""[1]

It is said that when he was introduced to the Tantra of Total Space (nam mkha' che) when he was eight years old, there was a shower of flowers. From then on, from Chen Zhikpo (gcen zhig po), Tokden Yangriwa (rtogs ldan g.yang ri ba), Lama Zhang, Deshek Tsetsawa (bde gshegs rtsad tsa ba), and Tanakpa Dorje Wobar (rta nag pa rdo rje 'od 'bar), he received instructions, commentaries, empowerments, blessings, guidance, and methods of the old and new tantras. In particular, from his father he received all of the instructions of the Rechung Nyengyu (ras chung snyan rgyud), or Aural Lineage of Rechungpa (ras chung pa rdo rje grags pa, 1085–1161), and it is said that he attained deep experience and realization in those practices.
Having received the teachings, he decided to set out to practice. His father told him,

We, father and son, are going to separate. Though we will not meet again, I have given you the entire set of instructions, with nothing left out. Your practice is good. The Aural Lineage is in the palm of your hand. I learned many teachings and looked after students. But since I spent a lot of time doing things like curing illnesses, I never became more than a middling meditator. You should concentrate on nothing but practicing the Aural Lineage. Later, through the power of your practice, you can start your own temple. This would be of immense benefit.[2]

With that, Sonam Gyeltsen went to Kongpo where he stayed for a year or two. During this time, he is said to have experienced many signs of accomplishment, such as a dream of subduing hostile spirits in Dzongkar (rdzong dkar).

Another time, while traveling through the pastures of Ormo Drang (or mog grang), there was a deadly outbreak of livestock disease. Sonam Gyeltsen fled by horse to toward Densatil Monastery (gdan sa mthil) before moving on to Tsang. While he was there, it is said that he had a dream of his father and saw that he had passed away.

He taught in Nyel (gnyal) and Loro (lo ro) and made his way to Tsang. There, he dedicated himself to practicing the Aural Lineage and it is said that he gained excellent realization in the practices of dream yoga (rmi lam) and illusory body (sgyu lus). According to his hagiography, many wondrous things happened such as that he was able to know the future through his practice of a secret Avalokiteśvara sādhana. Moreover, it is said that when he propitiated Vaiśravaṇa, he had a vision in which the deity gave him a bag containing a mongoose.
He founded a temple at Richung (ri chung), where his daughter, Kunden Rema (kun ldan ras ma), would later do retreat.

His hagiography records that once when he was praying to Lama Zhang, he had a vision of the guru surrounded by the four ḍākinīs. Lama Zhang pointed out to him the unborn essence of awareness and he prophesied that two worthy disciples would come to him. Also, he dreamed of being in a bedroom at Sakya Monastery (sa skya dgon) where he encountered Pakpa Lodro Gyeltsen ('phags pa blo gros rgyal mtshan, 1235–1280), whom he asked advice about meditation. Pakpa replied by giving him a letter and a golden statue. He is said to have innumerable visions of tutelary deities and dharma protectors and that after meeting his guru in dreams he resolved doubts he may have had about the Aural Lineage's Small Vajra Book (rdo rje gzhung chung)[i] and Mahāmudrā.

Legend has it that he could stop hail with flames from his fingertips and otherwise transform the weather. It is also said that he subdued many non-human spirits and put them on the path to dharma, that he came to the aid of many beings in the intermediate states between death and rebirth (bar do), and that he prophesied many future events.
His hagiography contains a statement that he gave his disciples at the age of fifty-eight:

From the time I was eighteen, I have known everything that would happen to me until I die. When I am seventy-six, I will start to become a little bit ill. You, my dear students, can perform non-stop sādhana pujas and fulfilment and confession rituals, and even if there are no signs of improvement, in all your future lives your minds will enjoy the state of clarity; you will be born into spiritual families; you will have excellent inclinations; you will be surrounded by the ripening and liberating white clouds of the Aural Lineage; and you will accomplish immense benefit for beings.[3]

Jangsem Choje Sonam Gyeltsen passed away at the age of seventy-six, as he is said to have predicted. Miracles are recorded to have occurred during his cremation: everyone present perceived a dome of rainbow light, and greenish-yellow birds appeared—larger than vultures—with markings of the sun and moon on their wings. Three times they circled the canopy above the cremation pyre, then flew off. Within the cremation kiln they found many relics (ring bsrel), religious images, syllables, and symbols, and statues of the Great and Glorious One (dpal chen po), Vajrasattva, Vajravidāraṇa, Avalokiteśvara, and Tārā.

Kunden Rema was a thirteenth-century teacher in the Aural Lineage of Rechungpa.

","

Kunden Rema was born in the Shang region of Tsang probably in the mid thirteenth century. She was the daughter of Jangsem Choje Sonam Gyeltsen (byang sems chos rje bsod nams rgyal mtshan)—a great meditator and holder of the Rechung Nyengyu (ras chung snyan rgyud), or Aural Lineage of Rechungpa (ras chung pa rdo rje grags pa, 1085–1161). She was also known as Yeshe Kunden (ye shes kun ldan) and Trulshik Kunden Rema ('khrul zhig kun ldan ras ma).

It is said that from a young age she was inclined to think about death and impermanence. She developed a strong sense of repulsion to saṃsāra and an intense resolve not to enter the life of a domestic woman.

When she was thirteen, she studied reading and writing and trained the rituals of the peaceful and wrathful deities. At fourteen, she began wandering in remote mountain retreats, dedicating her life to dharma practice. During this time, she encouraged her father to teach, saying,

Since you have done your practice and received teachings, and father, since you are still young, it is not right for you to stay in mountain retreats.  You seem like someone who is blessed by Vajravārāhī. I dreamed that a pig's head grew from the back of your neck and those around you trembled in humility at the sound of its grunting. It would be beneficial if you had a small group of students around you.[1]
She then had a vision of Rechungpa and was inspired to practice.

She is said to have had a vision of everything as golden light at the age of eighteen, and understood that at the conventional level, all phenomena were like illusions, while at the ultimate level, her mind itself could not be pinned down in any way. She thought, ""This unchanging native state—this is what I am."" From reading the Prajñāpāramitā in Eight Thousand Verses she came to perceive all the phenomena of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as illusory.

Her father was a tantric yogi without scholarly training—his own father had encouraged him to focus on practice over study[i]—and he taught her according to his own understanding. He warned her against taking disciples without further study, however, telling her,

When it comes to meditation, you can rely on yourself; but without rigorous learning, how could you nurture disciples? How can you perform empowerments and consecrations? Whatever arises in your mind, it is permissible to share that with disciples, but do not perform empowerment rituals or consecrations. Please make your practice genuine.[2]

With that said, he trained her in mantra and many sādhanas and practices of the new and old tantras. This training was specifically based on the Vajra Verses of the Aural Lineage (snyan brgyud rdo rje'i tshig rkang) the Small Book (gzung chung),[ii] Milarepa's (mi la ras pa, 1040–1143) secret guides (khrid yig sbas pa) and Khyung Tsangwa's (khyung tshang pa, 1115–1176) manuals. Finally, he bestowed all the empowerments and blessings for the father and mother deities (yab bka’ yum bka’) along with all their related pith instructions.

In addition to her father’s training, she is said to have received instructions from early Kagyu masters such the Second Karmapa, Karma Pakshi (karma pak+Shi, 1204–1283); the First Drukchen, Drubtob Gonye[iii] (grub thob mgon ye); Tarpa Lotsawa Nyima Gyeltsen (thar pa lo tsA ba nyi ma rgyal mtshan); Khedrub Choje (mkhas grub chos rje), and an unidentified figure with the epithet Dzamling Gyen ('dzam gling rgyan), ""Ornament of the World."" Her biography also states that she received teachings from Tropu Lotsāwa (khro phu lo tsa ba (c.1172–c.1236), however, it seems likely that he lived too early for them to have met directly.

Her father, who had accepted disciples, encouraged her to go into remote retreat, warning her that if she continued to wander the countryside she would probably end up with a husband. He suggested a place called Richung (ri chung) where she walled herself in isolation for a year.

On concluding her retreat, she went to the upper regions of Shang and eventually accepted disciples of her own. She next went to Zapulung (zab phu lung) where she practiced water austerity (chu’i dka’ thub) during which ghosts are said to have presented obstacles. As with other problems she had faced, she overcame them by taking them as allies to her meditation. One night, she dreamed that she was dressed in armor and brandishing a variety of weapons. As many ḍākinīs surrounded her, she slayed thousands of dreadlocked black men who were led by a non-Buddhist king. According to her hagiography, the result of the dream was that she had vanquished the four māras, or negative influences, and no obstacles could thereafter harm her. From then on, she no longer needed to isolate herself from towns, as she was no longer tempted by their charms. She developed a reputation as a Buddhist teacher and was sought after to cure illness in livestock and people.

She is said to have experienced multiple visions, including of Tārā and the buddhas of the three times, while practicing in Pumonkhar (phu smon mkhar) at Zhalu Monastery (zhwa lu dgon). She brought fifteen students on pilgrimage to U where they made offerings to the Jowo in the Lhasa Tsuklakhang (gtsug lag khang) at which point a rain of five-colored flowers is said to have fallen.

On returning to Shang, she entered retreat at a place called Gyere Drak (gye re'i brag). A lunar eclipse occurred while she was in retreat, during which she played the ḍāmaru drum and bell. According to her hagiography, when the eclipse reached totality, the cliff was rendered insubstantial and she fell uninjured through the rocks into the center of the mountain.

She is said to have composed numerous songs of experience, such as ""Entering the Solar and Lunar Path of Prāṇayāma"" (rlung srog rtsol nyi zla'i lam du tshud). Unfortunately, none of her songs are extant.

According to her hagiography, while teaching the Aural Lineage at Richung, during a gaṇacakra feast, everyone present saw a miraculous appearance: two purple vajras slowly rotated around the white rim of a ritual skull cup. In a state of joy, she told those present,

I did this because of your requests and entreaties. You kept asking me to show a sign of accomplishment, but from the time I was eighteen until my current age of seventy-five, I have practiced in remote solitudes. I am a lion that has roamed free under the unsupported sky. Is that not a sign of accomplishment?[3]

It is said that when she propitiated the protector deities, real fangs appeared on her face and she subdued all malevolent spirits, binding them with vows. She is said to have dedicated all donations she received to her dharma practice without any misappropriation, and that even though she had fully realized emptiness, she spared no effort when it came to engaging with the conditioned world.

She was able to meet Orgyenpa Rinchen Pel (o rgyan pa rin chen dpal, 1229–1309) while he was making his way to Mongolia. Orgyenpa is said to have been intrigued by her and asked her the year of her birth. Later on, he told a disciple, ""That woman is the reincarnation of Machik Drozang (ma gcig 'gro bzang), the disciple of Lord Gotsangpa Gonpo Dorje (rgod tshang pa mgon po rdo rje, 1189–1258). She has something obscuring her now. As soon as she clears that obscuration, she is going to be of immense benefit to beings.""[4]
Kunden Rema died at the age of eighty. Among her disciples was Kunpang Delek Rinchen (tsha bo kun spangs bde legs rin chen).

Kunpang Delek Rinchen was the son of the Eighth Sakya Trizin Rinchen Gyeltsen, who was the brother of Pakpa Lodro Gyeltsen. He was a student of Kunden Rema in the Aural Lineage of Rechungpa.

","

Kunpang Delek Rinchen (kun spangs bde legs rin chen) was born at Tsang Nyangro Monastery (gtsang myang ro'i dgon pa) as the son of the Eighth Sakya Tridzin, Rinchen Gyeltsen (sa skya tri 'dzin 08 rin chen rgyal mtshan, 1238–1279)—also known as Lama Richungpa (bla ma ri chung pa)—the younger brother of Pakpa Lodro Gyeltsen ('phags pa blo gros rgyal mtshan, 1235–1280). His father gave him the name Mipam Gyeltsen (mi pham rgyal mtshan).

According to his hagiography, he began reciting miscellaneous vajra verses when he was three years old. In front of a large assembly of people, it is said that he told his father, in impeccable honorific language, that he recognized the cup that was in front of him from his previous life as Lama Sonam Gyeltsen (bsod nams rgyal mtshan).

He learned to read and write quickly. His father gave him empowerments and trained him in their sādhanas. Despite his youth, it is said that he was able to understand everything that was taught to him.

From 1270–1274, after decades of involvement with the Mongolian rulers, his uncle Pakpa Lodro Gyeltsen served as imperial preceptor to Kublai Khan (reigned 1260–1294) in Beijing. Kunpang Delek Rinchen's biography states that when he was nine years old— around 1269 or 1272—his father was also summoned to Beijing as an imperial preceptor, apparently overlapping with Pakpa, perhaps in a deputy capacity. Kunpang Delek Rinchen remained in Tibet and went to train under Drinchen Kunden Rema (drin chen kun ldan ras ma). From her he received empowerments in the Nyingma tradition and trained in the sādhanas for the peaceful and wrathful deities. These included empowerments and teachings for the Guhyagarbha Tantra, which he received when he was twelve years old. In particular, Kunden Rema bestowed on him the empowerments and instructions for the Rechung Nyengyu (ras chung snyan rgyud), or Aural Lineage of Rechungpa (ras chung pa, 1085–1161).

From Tarpa Lotsāwa (thar pa lo tsA ba), Tropu Panchen Shakya Sengge (khro phu paN chen shAkya seng+ge), Lopon Gyalwa Zangpo (slob dpon rgyal ba bzang po), and a Lama Ārya (bla ma Ar+ya) he received teachings in the new and old traditions and practiced under their guidance.
He received lay vows and the name Lodro Gyeltsen (blo gros rgyal mtshan) from the Eleventh Sakya Trizin, Daknyi Chenpo (sa skya khri 'dzin 11 bdag nyid chen po, 1262–1324).

When Kunpang Delek Rinchen was nineteen, around 1279 or 1282, word was sent that his father had fallen ill in China. He traveled to Beijing arrived only after his father had passed away. The Yuan emperor at the time, Kublai Khan, gave him gifts and spoke favorably of his father.

On his return to Tibet, he took monastic ordination and enrolled in a retreat center at Samding Monastery (bsam sdings). There, Zhonnu Sonam (gzhon nu bsod nams) honored him with the title of khenpo (mkhan po), or ""master scholar,"" and Rinchen Chok (rin chen mchog) gave him the title of lopon (slob dpon), or ""master teacher.""

At the age of twenty-six, he took full bhikṣu ordination and received the name Delek Rinchen. To each member of the saṇgha he offered half a zho (zho) of gold and half a sang (srang) of silver. To the five khenpos he gave nine sang  and to the lopons three. Under these circumstances, he received initiation into the mahāsiddha Vajraghatapada's Cakrasaṃvara lineage and other traditions held at the monastery. After being guided in Mahāmudrā, the Six Yogas of Nāropa, and subtle body practices, it is said that his meditative experience flourished. He also received Lamdre (lam 'bras) and Richo (ri chos) teachings, an indication of the eclectic teachings available at Samding at the time. It is said that in every one of his practice sessions, he never failed to make fine offerings to the objects of refuge.

After that period of training, he returned to his guru, Kunden Rema, and in three different session received all of the empowerments, guidance, and pith instructions that she had not bestowed on him previously. It is then that he became a holder of Rechungpa’s Aural Lineage.

He received teachings from a Lama Jamyang (bla ma 'jam dbyangs), Kachopa (mkha' spyod pa), and Joden Khenchen Sonam Drakpa (jo gdan mkhen chen bsod nams grags pa). On separate occasions, he offered all three of them everything he owned. He also decided to give up his residence and enter strict mountain retreat in the Lato region of Tsang, where for one year he practiced austerities in the high forests.

After that, he journeyed to Dropuk (grod phug) in Nyanang or Nyenam (gnya' nang / snye nam) and the ""Six Fortresses"" (rdzong drug) in Kyirong (skyid rong)—all sacred sites associated with Milarepa. He also went to Labchi (la phyi), a massive mountain range on Tibet's southern border, with the intention of remaining for many years. At Labchi he wore only cotton robes. It is said that by corralling the winds of karma (las rlung) into the central channel, he was able to halt the flow of his subtle energies and rest in nonconceptual meditative absorption. Legend has it that at the Cave of the Subjugation of Māra (bdud 'dul phug), within an ongoing meditative state of luminosity, he visited the Sukhāvatī pure land, where he encountered two thousand buddhas. It is also said that while staying in a secret cave associated with Rechungpa, he had visions of the Kagyu masters, yidam deities, and dharma protectors.
Three years into his residence at Labchi he received a letter from his mother, who had lost her eyesight. He therefore returned home to care for her.

Kunpang Delek Rinchen's foremost disciple was Ketsun Ziji Gyeltsen (mkhas btsun gzi brjid rgyal mtshan) who accompanied him in the Labchi mountains. When Ketsun Ziji Gyaltsen met Kunden Rema herself, she bestowed on him the empowerments and instructions of the Aural Lineage.

Jomo Auma of Yalung was a disciple of Sachen Kunga Nyingpo, for whom he composed a commentary on the core Lamdre text Vajra Verses. She is counted among three female students of Sachen along with Jomo Purmo and Jomo Mangchungma.

","

Jomo Auma of Yalung (g.ya' lung) was presumably a twelfth-century practitioner. Sachen Kunga Nyingpo (sa chen kun dga' snying po, 1092–1158) is believed to have composed the Auma ('a 'u ma)—one his eleven commentaries on the Vajra Verses (rdo rje tshig rkang) of Virupa—for her. Her name comes from her having howled like a dog—""aoo""—while meditating, which commentators have taken to mean that she had been a dog in a previous life. Nesar Jamyang Khyentse Wangchuk (gnas gsar 'jam dbyangs mkhyen brtse'i dbang phyug, 1524–1568) wrote that her howling was a sign of her purifying past karma that would have caused her to be reborn as a dog.[1]

According to Cyrus Stearns, a eulogy to Sachen by his student Zhuje Ngodrub (zhu byas dngos grub) contained a list of eight men and three women. The Twenty-First Sakya Tridzin, Lodro Gyeltsen (bdag chen blo gros rgyal mtshan, 1444–495), understood this to refer to the eleven commentaries, and Jomo Auma is considered among one of three female students of Sachen along with Jocham Purmo (jo mo 'a 'u ma) and Jomo Mangchungma (jo mo mang chung ma). Later scholars, including Mangto Lhundrub Gyatso (mang thos klu sgrub rgya mtsho, 1523–1596) and Nesar Jamyang Khyentse Wangchuk (gnas gsar 'jam dbyangs mkhyen brtse'i dbang phyug, 1524–1568) based their lists of the eleven commentaries on this eulogy, although there are other lists containing only ten commentaries and recipients.[2]

Jomo Mangchuma was a disciple of Sachen Kunga Nyingpo, who is said to have dedicated to her one of eleven commentaries on the Vajra Verses (rdo rje tshig rkang) of Virupa, a core text of the Lamdre tradition.

","

Jomo Mangchungma (jo mo mang chung pa) of Mangkhar (mang mkhar) was presumably a twelfth-century practitioner. Her identity is linked to the Mangchungma, one of eleven commentaries written by Sachen Kunga Nyingpo (sa chen kun dga' snying po, 1092–1158) on the Vajra Verses (rdo rje tshig rkang) of Virupa, a core text of the Lamdre tradition.

According to Cyrus Stearns, a eulogy to Sachen by his student Zhuje Ngodrub (zhu byas dngos grub) contained a list of eight men and three women. The Twenty-First Sakya Tridzin, Lodro Gyeltsen (bdag chen blo gros rgyal mtshan, 1444–1495), understood this list to refer to the eleven commentaries, and Jomo Mangchungma is generally considered to have been one of three female students of Sachen along with Jocham Auma (jo mo 'a 'u ma) and Jocham Purmo (jo lcam phur mo). Later scholars, including Mangto Lhundrub Gyatso (mang thos klu sgrub rgya mtsho, 1523–1596) and Nesar Jamyang Khyentse Wangchuk (gnas gsar 'jam dbyangs mkhyen brtse'i dbang phyug, 1524–1568) based their lists of the eleven commentaries on the eulogy listing, although there are other enumerations, some containing only ten commentaries.[1]

Nesar Jamyang Khyentse Wangchuk wrote that while in meditation Jomo Mangchungma howled, having experienced being a yak, and thus was purified from birth in that realm. Stearns notes that this echoes the experience of Jomo Auma, another of Sachen's students, who was said to have experienced being a dog at some point.[2]

Because the Mangchungma is no longer extant, some Tibetan historians have argued that the commentary never existed and that it is the same as the Auma ('a 'u ma) commentary intended for Jomo Auma. This position thereby calls into question the historicity of Jomo Mangchungma.

Jocham Purmo, also known as Machik Tsetsa, was the first wife and disciple of Sachen Kunga Nyingpo, for whom he may have composed the Yumdonma, a commentary on the core Lamdre text Vajra Verses. After the death of her eldest son, she became a devoted practitioner. According to some sources, she is counted among three female students of Sachen along with Jomo Auma and Jomo Mangchungma.

","

Jocham Purmo (jo lcam phur mo) was born into the prominent Jetse (rje btsad) family, a clan from Tsamorong (tsha mo rong). She is also known as Machik Tsetsa. She was married to Sachen Kunga Nyingpo (sa chen kun dga' snying po, 1092–1158) with whom she had one son, Kunga Bar (kun dga' 'bar). Sachen later married Jocham Purmo's older sister, Machik Wodron (ma gcig 'od sgron), who was the mother of his three other sons.[1]

Kunga Bar traveled to India and distinguished himself as a scholar but died while on his journey home to Tibet. After his death, Jocham Purmo became a devoted practitioner. The Yumdonma (yum don ma), one of Sachen's eleven commentaries on the Vajra Verses (rdo rje tshig rkang) of Virupa, may have been composed for her benefit. Cyrus Stearns notes that there was some confusion as to the attribution of this commentary, which is focused on Cakrasaṃvara practice. A Derge edition suggests it was written for Sachen's mother, Machik Zhangmo (ma gcig zhang mo).

According to Cyrus Stearns, a eulogy to Sachen by his student Zhuje Ngodrub (zhu byas dngos grub) contained a list of eleven disciples: eight men and three women. The Twenty-First Sakya Tridzin, Lodro Gyeltsen (blo gros rgyal mtshan, 1444–1495), understood this to refer to the eleven commentaries, and Jocham Purmo is considered among one of the three female students of Sachen along with Jomo Auma (jo mo 'a 'u ma) and Jomo Mangchungma (jo mo mang chung ma). Later scholars, including Mangto Lhundrub Gyatso (mang thos klu sgrub rgya mtsho, 1523–1596) and Nesar Jamyang Khyentse Wangchuk (gnas gsar 'jam dbyangs mkhyen brtse'i dbang phyug, 1524–1568), based their lists of the eleven commentaries on this eulogy, although there are other lists, some of which only contain ten commentaries and recipients.[2]

Khaying Drolma was an early nineteenth-century practitioner. She was the daughter of Do Khyentse Yeshe Dorje and married Tsewang Rabten, the king of Trokyab in Gyarong.

","

Khaying Drolma was born in the winter of 1823 at the Sarwahai Hermitage (sar ba ha'i ri khrod) at Drongdzong (grong rdzong) in the region of Gyelmo Tsarong (rgyal mo tsha rong). She was the daughter of Do Khyentse Yeshe Dorje (mdo mkhyen brtse ye shes rdo rje, 1800–1866) and Akyong Bumo Dzompa Kyi (a skyong bu mo 'dzom pa skyid). Her aunt was Ḍākki Losel Drolma (DAk+ki blo gsal sgrol ma, 1802–1861). From the time of her birth, Khaying Drolma was considered an emanation of the eight-century saint Yeshe Tsogyel (ye shes mtsho rgyal).

She learned reading, writing, and chanting from Do Khyentse and his sister, Losel Drolma. From them she also received empowerments, scriptural transmissions, and guiding instructions. She accompanied them to places such as Do Dzong Hermitage (rdo rdzong ri khrod) and Nechen Pema Hermitage (gnas chen pad+ma ri khrod) in Golok; Zhakdra Turquoise Lake (bzhag bra g.yu mtsho) in Minyak; Kardza Hermitage (dkar mdza' ri khrod); Pelri Monastery (dpal ri dgon); Lautang Monastery (la'u thang dgon); and Mahā Kyilung Monastery (ma hA skyid lung dgon) in the region of Geshe Gyelpo.

In 1841, when she was nineteen years old, her family arranged for her to marry Tsewang Rabten (tshe dbangs rab brtan), the king of Trokyab (khro skyabs), the most powerful of the eighteen kingdoms in Gyarong based in the capital city of Mutri Pelek (dmu khrid dpal legs). The king was a faithful Buddhist practitioner and Do Khyentse wished to usher in a golden age for the spread of the Nyingma Nyingtik (snying thig) and Tuktik (thugs thig) teachings in the region. The wedding did not take place, however, until 1849. Do Khyentse himself did not escort her to the capital, but the ceremonies were carried out by members of his retinue.

In the years that followed, the king received all the Nyingtik and Tuktik empowerments and guiding instructions from Ḍākki Losel Drolma and Do Khyentse. It is said that his understanding and experience flourished and Do Khyentse entrusted him as a lineage holder.

In 1852, when Khaying Drolma was thirty, she came down with a severe illness. It was said that she was poisoned by followers of the Bon tradition who were jealous of the family's influence on the court. Extensive medical treatment and rituals were not able to help her. When it was clear that her recovery was not immanent, Do Khyentse went to Trokyab to perform rituals, but they too were not effective.

In 1853, Do Khyentse and Losel Drolma went again to Trokyab to counsel Khaying Drolma and perform rituals for her health. They then left for Tseten Ling (tshe brtan gling) in Gartok, where they were engaged in teaching activities. At the Trokyab king's request, Losel Drolma returned to the capital once more that year to perform more rituals and give more counsel to Khaying Drolma.

In 1854, Do Khyentse and Losal Drolma returned to the Trokyab capital as Khaying Drolma's health deteriorated. Do Khyentse made aspirations, guided her through the paths and levels, and gave her special empowerments in preparation of her death. It is said that Khaying Drolma had no fear of dying and remained in a joyful state of mind. On the fifteenth day of the second month, she passed away, showing unmistakable signs of accomplishing the transference of consciousness.

After her passing, the Trokyab ruler, Do Khyentse, Losel Drolma, and hosts of lamas and tulkus came to the capital for her funeral services. It is said that at the time of the cremation, the sky thickened with rainbow-hued clouds and vultures circled. Losel Drolma stayed to oversee the collection of her relics, then she rejoined Do Khyentse at Tseten Ling. It was at that time after the cremation that Losel Drolma dreamed of girl dressed in white silk who said,

My emanation was in Tibet, but the ground of my emanation is going to purify its obscurations and receive the fruitional empowerment from Guru Rinpoche on the southwestern continent of Camaradvipa (rnga yab gling).

In a past life, during a teaching at the Śaṅkarakūṭa Stūpa (bde byed brtsegs pa), a worldly ḍākinī cursed me, which prevented me from benefitting beings to my full potential here in the human realm. Although I was not able to fulfill all the king's wishes, because of me he was able to consummate his practice of Tuktik and he will join me in the vidyādharas' pure land.
My emanation and its ground are one, but now, like the moon reflected in limpid water, I will return again to fulfill the wishes of my brothers and sisters and to further the practice of Tuktik.
Tsewang Rabten built a reliquary stupa for Khaying Drolma, which Do Khyentse consecrated.

Khaying Drolma had only lived in the Trokyab capital for six years, and she and the king were not able to produce any children. Half a year after her death, Do Khyentse recognized her reincarnation as Somang Tulku (so mang mchog sprul; 1855-c.1935), the son of Dechen Rigpai Reltri (bde chen rig pa'i ral gri) and Sonam Wangmo (bsod nams dbang mo), a noblewoman from the Somang (so mang) kingdom of Gyarong.

Pema Tseden was an author and filmmaker who made an indelible mark in the world of modern Tibetan cinema with masterpieces such as Old Dog and Tharlo. Not only did he bring Tibetan voices to the attention of international cinema, but he also influenced, inspired, and supported a generation of Tibetan filmmakers. He skillfully navigated government involvement in his films, managing to highlight issues of Tibetan cultural importance. A prolific artist whose works included three collections of short stories and twenty films, Pema Tseden died suddenly in 2023 of heart failure while filming near Yamdrok Yumtso.

","

Pema Tseden was born in December 1969 in the village of Trika Lhakhang Tang (khri kha lha khang thang), part of the Tsolho Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture (mtsho lho rang skyong khul) in Amdo. He attended primary and secondary schools in Trika. When he was nine years old, his parents divorced, and his mother remarried, leaving Pema and his siblings behind; their grandfather took on the responsibility of raising them. Following his secondary school education, he enrolled in the Tibetan Teacher's Training College (mi rigs dge thon slob grwa) in Chabcha county (chab cha rdzong). This was one of many training colleges that had been established under the leadership of the famous scholar Sungrab Gyatso (gsung rab rgya mtsho, 1896-1982).

After finishing his studies, Pema Tseden returned to his village and spent four years as a Tibetan language teacher at a primary school. In 1991, he was accepted into Northwest Minzu University in Lanzhou to pursue his undergraduate degree, majoring in Tibetan language and literature.  Upon graduation, he worked for the local government in his hometown for five years. Subsequently, he applied to Northwest Minzu University to pursue a master's degree in Tibetan-Chinese translation, which he completed within two years.
In 1994, Pema Tseden married Youdon Tso (gyu sgron mtsho), a Tibetan medical doctor. Their son Jigme Trinle ('jigs med 'phrin las) was born in 1997. He is also a filmmaker.
Contributions to Tibetan Literature

Pema Tseden's fascination with literature and films began to take root at a young age. While in primary school, he had the opportunity to watch Charlie Chaplin movies, which were screened by the local government. This ignited a passion within him that he carried for many years, fueling his love for storytelling.

During the early 1990s, he embarked on his journey as a writer, crafting short stories in Tibetan and later in Chinese. While an undergraduate at Northwest Minzu University, he published a story titled ""Man and Dog"" (mi dang khyi) in the journal Tibetan Art and Literature (bod kyi rtsom rig sgyu rtsal). Continuing his creative endeavors, he published ""A Story and Two Ways of Concluding It"" (btsams sgrung zhig dang de'i mjug bsdu tshul gnyis) in Qinghai People's Literature (mtsho sngon mang tshogs sgyu rtsal) in 1994. Two years later, ""A Winter Without Snow"" (kha ba med pa'i dgun kha) found its way into the same publication, thanks to the assistance of his friend Rangda (rang sgra, b. 1964), the magazine's editor.

In subsequent years, he produced a substantial body of written work, including numerous short stories many of which contained magical realism. Among his notable creations are ""Snow"" (gangs), ""The Dream of a Wandering Minstrel"" (yul gyur rdung len pa zhig gi rmi lam), ""Interview of Aku Thopa"" (a khu thod pa la btsar 'drir phrin pa),  ""Grassland"" (rtswa thang), ""City Life"" (grong khyer gyi 'tsho ba), ""Depression"" (sems nad), ""Beggar"" (slong mo ba), ""Red Scarf""(ske dkri dmar po), ""Ugen's Teeth"" (o rgyan gyi so), and ""Tharlo"" (thar lo). Many of his stories were eventually compiled into three collections. Enticement (bslu brid) was published in 2009 by Qinghai Nationalities Publishing House; City Life was released by Tibet People's Publishing House in 2012; the third collection, Pema Tseden's Short Stories, was published in 2018.

His remarkable short stories have been translated into various languages, including English, Chinese, French, German, Spanish, Japanese, Korean, and Czech. Notably, the collection Enticement: Stories of Tibet was translated into English by Patricia Schiaffini-Vedani and Michael Monhart in 2018, making his work accessible to a wide international audience.  The stories ""Enticement,"" ""Snow,"" ""Ugen's Teeth,"" and ""City Life"" garnered significant acclaim and achieved popularity among Tibetan, Chinese, and other readers across the globe. These stories resonated deeply with diverse audiences, transcending cultural boundaries.
A Tibetan Approach to Cinema

While pursuing his MA in Tibetan literature at Northwest Minzu University in the early 2000s, Pema Tseden crossed paths with his friend Gangzhun (gangs zhun, b. 1969), also known as Gangchuk (gangs phyugs), who was studying in the same field. Upon completing his degree, Gangzhun secured a position at the nonprofit Trace Foundation's office in Xining. It was through Gangzhun that Pema Tseden became aware of a scholarship opportunity for film studies. Pema Tseden was awarded a two-year grant to study directing and scriptwriting at the prestigious Beijing Film Academy. This scholarship marked a pivotal moment in his career as he first ventured into the world of filmmaking. The Trace Foundation played a crucial role in supporting Pema Tseden's filmmaking journey, as he himself has acknowledged.

In late 2004, Gangzhun, along with others, established an organization called Himalaya Culture and Arts Limited (hi ma la ya rig gnas sgyu rtsal tshad yod kung si). This organization became instrumental in producing Pema Tseden's films, including some of his most notable works, such as The Silent Holy Stones (lhing 'jags kyi ma Ni rdo 'bum), Old Dog (khyi rgan), Tharlo (thar lo),and Jinpa (sbyin pa). The collaborative efforts between Pema Tseden and Himalaya Culture and Arts Limited laid the foundation for his burgeoning success in the world of cinema.

In 2004, Pema Tseden released his first film, Grassland (rtswa thang), specifically made for the University Film Festival. This thirty-minute short film was adapted from his short story of the same name. Set in rural Tibet, it depicts the journey of an elderly nomadic couple in search of a stolen yak, which they had recently set free from domestication.

Around 2005, Pema Tseden released his first full-length feature, The Silent Holy Stones, which he wrote and directed. Also based on one of his own short stories, the film revolves around a ten-year-old Buddhist monk who returns home from a remote monastery to celebrate the Tibetan New Year. After a lengthy journey on horseback, he becomes engrossed by his family's new television, captivated by the popular Chinese series Journey to the West. Meanwhile, the villagers in his hometown prepare for their annual performance of a traditional Tibetan opera. Written entirely in Tibetan and featuring nonprofessional Tibetan actors, the film explores the intersection of tradition and modernity within the context of China's influence. It was one of the first films out of Tibet and its success introduced Pema Tseden to the international community.

In 2005 and 2006, The Silent Holy Stones received nominations at various international film festivals and garnered multiple awards, including the Best Directorial Debut at the twenty-fifth Golden Rooster Awards, the Chinese equivalent of the Academy Awards; the New Current Award at the tenth Busan International Film Festival; Best Director at the eighth Changchun Film Festival; and Best First Feature at the thirteenth Beijing College Student Film Festival.

Following his studies in directing and scriptwriting at the Beijing Film Academy, Pema Tseden pursued another year of study at the same institution before embarking on his next film, The Search ('tshol), released in 2009. The film follows a director, his assistant, and a businessman as they travel from village to village in Tibet's Amdo region, searching for actors to feature in a film based on the Tibetan opera Drime Kunden (dri med kun ldan), based on the Indian Buddhist legend of Prince Vessantara, who sacrifices his children and even his own eyes for the sake of others. The Search received nominations at several international film festivals, including the seventh Bangkok International Film Festival, the twenty-fifth Warsaw International Film Festival, and the fifty-third London International Film Festival.

Pema Tseden was heavily influenced by Tibetan oral literature and local cultures and it is those qualities that make his films distinctly Tibetan. Both The Silent Holy Stones and The Search draw inspiration from the stories he grew up hearing, such as the Gesar epics, Tibetan operas, Buddhist parables, and the Tale of the Golden Corpse (mi ro rtse sgrung), a well known Tibetan folk tale. Pema Tseden grew up hearing these stories, which greatly influenced his worldview. Additionally, both films prominently feature themes related to the legendary Tibetan opera figure Drime Kunden. In the case of The Search, the idea emerged from a love story told to Pema Tseden by a businessman many years prior. This same individual later became a character in the film. While making this film, Pema Tseden and his team encountered an old man who was said to have offered to give his wife to another man, as Drime Kunden himself does in the folktale.

In both films, Pema Tseden's visual style was largely influenced by Tibetan thangka (thang ka) paintings; he spoke about the powerful imagery of thangkas in numerous appearances and interviews. In particular, he described how he was fascinated by the ability of these paintings to convey the entirety of the Buddha's life on a single canvas. In his subsequent films, Pema Tseden frequently employed long takes to create meaningful distance between the camera, characters, and environment. This technique allowed him to create a view of contemporary Tibetan society in which environmental phenomena hold more significance than facial expressions and individual characters. The use of extended shots of small figures framed by the landscape aims to visually evoke the traditional aesthetic commonly observed in thangka paintings.

In the early stages of his career, Pema Tseden established additional foundational principles that served as the backbone of his later filmmaking. His films aimed to portray contemporary Tibetan society, and he preferred to shoot them in Tibetan environments, employing Tibetan actors even if it meant they had no professional training. He believed that the deep, subtle, and authentic worldview, experiences, and cultural exposure of locals surpassed that of professional actors who lacked a native upbringing. Furthermore, he insisted on making his films in the Tibetan language.

Old Dog, released in 2011, is a brilliant film that tells the story of a father and son against the backdrop of China's once thriving trade in Tibetan mastiffs. It serves as a tragic allegory for the erosion of Tibetan culture under the contemporary Chinese economy, in which traditional Tibetan values clash with external forces.

The film's production was hindered by the same forces it depicts. Permission from the Chinese government to shoot the film was delayed. Before filming could begin, the dog initially chosen for the film passed away and the house selected for the set was destroyed by the local government for a road construction project. When permission was finally granted, Pema Tseden had to find a new dog and a different location. He had intentionally selected a Tibetan town undergoing significant redevelopment, one which had also been a target of political revolt during the Cultural Revolution. Some locales still bear revolutionary names, such as ""Red Flag"" and ""Liberation."" By paying attention to the background noise and bustling environment, the audience can observe the transformations occurring in this small town. Additionally, the film's ending had two versions—one for Chinese audiences and another for international audiences. In the international version, the old man eventually kills the old dog, preventing Chinese vendors from purchasing it and others from stealing it. In the Chinese version, in response to a request from the government, the man does not kill the dog. Old Dog received numerous accolades, including Best Picture at the twelfth Tokyo Future International Film Festival and Best Native Feature at the Brooklyn Film Festival.

In 2015, Pema Tseden released Tharlo, an adaptation of a short story he wrote in 2013 for the literary journal Qinghai. Beautifully rendered in black and white, the film presents an elliptical tale of a protagonist caught between Chinese state bureaucracy and Tibetan spirituality. Tharlo, a Tibetan shepherd, leads a simple life away from urban areas, spending his days caring for his sheep and enjoying the comfort of riding his motorcycle. However, his tranquil nomadic lifestyle takes an unforeseen twist when he embarks on a journey to the city to acquire a photograph for his ID card. It is during this excursion that he unexpectedly comes across Yangtso (gyang mtsho), a young hairdresser. This encounter profoundly and permanently alters the trajectory of Tharlo's life.

The two lead roles were played by the popular singer Yangchuk Tso (gyang phyug mtsho) and the accomplished comedian Shide Nyima (zhi bde nyi ma). Yangchuk Tso had previously had a small part in Pema Tseden's The Silent Holy Stones. In 2015, when Pema Tseden was searching for a female actor for Tharlo, he met with Yangchuk Tso in Beijing. Initially, he considered her physically too thin for the role, but she insisted on reading the script. Later, they met again at the airport, discovered they were on the same flight and sat next to each other. They discussed the female character over the course of the two-hour journey, and Yangchuk Tso, although still expressing interest in the part and willing to gain weight for it, recommended two Tibetan actors. A few days later, Pema Tseden offered her the chance to audition and ultimately gave her the role. Tharlo received nominations at numerous international film festivals and won several awards, including the Paris Oriental Language Award at the twenty-second Visual Asia International Film Festival and the Best Film award at the sixteenth Tokyo Filmex.

As a Tibetan, and especially as a minority artist in China, when his films started drawing global attention, it was perhaps inevitable that he would face a variety of challenges from the authorities. On June 25, 2016, Pema Tseden was travelling from Beijing to Xining when he was apprehended by the police at Xining airport in Qinghai province. The police accused him of ""disrupting social order"" after he had inadvertently left a piece of luggage in the departure hall. During the incident, he was grabbed by the hair and sustained numerous bruises. He was subjected to overnight interrogation on June 26, causing him to experience vertigo, chest congestion, and finger numbness. On the afternoon of June 27, he was admitted to the hospital. Pema Tseden shared with many friends his belief that the airport incident severely damaged his reputation. A university in Hong Kong had previously offered him a professorship, but the offer was canceled following the incident, although it is unknown whether this was due to pressure from the Chinese government or concerns from within the university. He later filed a lawsuit against the police for defamation, but no apology was issued. The authorities sent a retired Tibetan policeman to persuade him to drop the case but he refused, and it remains unresolved. He kept a journal documenting the incident that has not been published.

In 2018, Pema Tseden released Jinpa (sbyin pa), which draws inspiration from two short stories: ""The Slayer"" by Tsering Norbu and one of Pema Tseden's own stories, ""I Ran Over a Sheep"" (lug gcig bsad pa). The narrative revolves around Jinpa, a truck driver who accidentally runs over a sheep while driving along a remote road on the Tibetan Plateau. Soon after, he crosses paths with a young hitchhiker who seeks revenge against the person responsible for his father's killing ten years earlier. Although the two men are on separate journeys, the link between the two events lingers in Jinpa's mind. Motivated by a determination to prevent the impending murder, he sets out on a mission to find the hitchhiker. The film prompts viewers to reexamine their comprehension of spirituality, morality, and reality. Pema Tseden employs a distinct visual approach in Jinpa, utilizing three color palettes to differentiate between reality, memories (presented in black and white) and dreams (presented with a soft focus).

For Jinpa, Pema Tseden cast three main actors hailing from different regions of Tibet. Sonam Wangmo (bsod nams dbang mo) from Lhasa, Jinpa (sbyin pa) from Amdo, and Gedun Phuntsok (dge 'dun phun tshogs) from Kham. Sonam Wangmo and Jinpa underwent training to speak the Khampa dialects, thus avoiding the customary use of voice-over actors. To understand his character, Jinpa even embarked on a journey, driving through various parts of Tibet to experience the life of a driver amidst the vast landscapes of the plateau. Similarly, in preparation for his role, Gendun Puntsok disguised himself as a beggar and spent several days traveling to different villages, immersing himself in the life of homelessness. While filming a momo-eating scene, Jinpa consumed over forty-five momos in order to provide the desired shot. The film received numerous nominations at international film festivals and garnered several accolades, including the award for Best Screenplay at the seventy-fifth Venice International Film Festival.

In 2019, Pema Tseden released Balloon (dbugs lgang), which delves into the struggles faced by a Tibetan family caught between religious conservatism and government policies. The initial inspiration for the film came to Pema Tseden when he witnessed a balloon floating in the sky while walking through Zhongguancun, Beijing's technology hub. From there, he transformed the concept into a Tibetan story set against the backdrop of the 1990s, a period marked by the Chinese government's one-child policy. The story centers on Dolkar (sgrol dkar) and her husband, sheep farmers raising three sons. In order to comply with the one-child policy, Dolkar turns to condoms as a form of birth control, a practice that deviates from the norms of traditional Tibetan society. Their circumstances exemplify the conflicting demands arising from nature, spirituality, governmental politics, and the concept of individual liberty.

The screenplay for Balloon was initially penned around 2012, but it faced a prolonged approval process. In the original script, two female characters held equal prominence. Notably, a nun, played by Yangchuk Tso, served as the main female protagonist, and the narrative revolved around her journey from the monastery to her home, encountering familial loss and other challenges along the way, while contemplating the cyclical nature of existence. Pema Tseden even requested Yangchuk Tso to spend several months in a nunnery to gain firsthand insights for the role. However, the script underwent multiple revisions, resulting in the nun's character assuming a minor role in the final version. Balloon received nominations at various international film festivals and won Best Screenplay at the fifth Chicago International Film Festival and the twentieth Tokyo Filmex.

Over the last two decades of his life, Pema Tseden produced more than twenty movies including several that were government-sponsored, such as Kathok Monlam Chenmo (kaH thog smon lam chen mo, 2007), Samye Monastery (bsam yas, 2007), and The Sacred Arrow (mda' lha 2014). These films are available on Chinese streaming platforms.
Legacy and Death

Pema Tseden revolutionized contemporary Tibetan cinema by expanding the reach of the Tibetan narrative on a global scale, as well as by inspiring a new generation of filmmakers. He served as a guiding influence and mentor for numerous Tibetan filmmakers, supporting the creation of movies such as Sonthar Gyal's River (gtsang po), Lhapal Gyal's Wangdak's Rain Boots (dbang grags kyi chu lham), Khashem Gyal's The Daughter of Light (me tog dkar po), Jigme Trinley's One and Four (gcig dang bzhi), Tashi Choephel's Ganglha Metok (gangs lha me tog), Lhoten's The Long Journey to Lhasa (dbum lam ring mo), Samdup Tsering's The Sky of Tanito (ta’i ni stod kyi nam mkha') and others. His enduring legacy continues to motivate these filmmakers to share the rich, untold Tibetan stories with the rest of the world.

On May 1, 2023, Pema Tseden embarked on a trip to Lhasa, specifically to Nakartse (sna dkar rtse rdzong) near Yamdrok Yumtso (yar 'brog gyu mtsho), situated over 4,450 meters above sea level. His purpose was to support his son, Jigme Trinle, who was directing a new film titled Karma and the Path (las dang lam), for which Pema Tseden had written the script. Pema Tseden undertook this journey without the company of his usual assistants, including his nephew, who typically attended to his health and medical requirements.

There were approximately 130 individuals involved in the production, and the shooting location was based in a small town, with crew members accommodated in various hotels. On the night of May 7, 2023, Pema Tseden stayed at Xinhu Hotel, occupying a room on the third floor. Unfortunately, he did not receive the usual supply of oxygen that each crew member normally receives when shooting a movie at high altitudes. Additionally, according to witnesses, the temperature in his room was excessively hot.

Pema Tseden's friend, Tsemdo (tshe mdo) was staying at a different hotel. At around 3:16 am, Pema Tseden contacted Tsemdo, requesting assistance. Tsemdo promptly went to Pema Tseden's hotel, and the two of them ordered a taxi to transport them to the nearby hospital. When they arrived outside the hospital at approximately 3:39 am, Pema Tseden managed to take a few steps before vomiting and collapsing. Tsemdo's efforts to support him proved futile. Eventually, the taxi driver and another individual helped transport Pema Tseden to the emergency room, but he had already passed away. His death was attributed to heart failure.

Efforts were made to arrange for a helicopter to transport his body to Lhasa. When this plan failed, Tsemdo and others took the responsibility of driving his body to the Lhasa People's Hospital, where medical professionals officially confirmed his death at 7:57 am. Subsequently, his body was taken to the residence of a former classmate, Tsering Gyal (tshe ring rgyal), where traditional Tibetan funeral rituals were performed.

On the morning of May 10, at 4:30 am, Pema Tseden's body was transported by the local funeral service company to the Jokhang Temple (lha sa tsug lag khang) for kora (bskor ba), or circumambulation. Over 200 people gathered in the vicinity of Jokhang Temple to offer their final respects. Afterward, the production company took his body to the funeral home at the Tolung Dechen Rinchen Gang (stod lung bde chen rin chen sgang) cremation site. In the afternoon of May 10, Pema Tseden's ashes were brought to Amdo Trika, his birthplace, by his son and friends.

Prior to his passing, Pema Tseden had completed two films, Snow Leopard (gsa') and Sing Pangta (sing spang bkra), which have not yet been released as of this writing. He had achieved excellence and renown as both a writer and a filmmaker, kickstarting Tibetan filmmaking inside Tibet, and moreover, inspiring and encouraging a new generation of Tibetan filmmakers. Tibetan filmmaker Tenzing Sonam, who lives in Dharamsala, called Pema Tseden a ""pioneering filmmaker who spearheaded the new Tibetan cinema inside Tibet against all odds.""

Upon his passing, the global community mourned his loss, and Tibetans held forty-nine-day memorials not only in Tibet but in places as far as Dharamsala and New York. His death was covered by over 250 news outlets, including The New York Times and The Economist.

The Ladakhi Amchi Tashi Yangphel Tashigang was trained in Tibetan medicine in Lhasa and later became a famous scholar of Tibetan medical literature, working under E. Gene Smith at the Library of Congress in Delhi. He independently published more than 250 volumes of Tibetan astrological and medical texts in the Smanrtsis Shesrig Spendzod series between 1969 and 1989. He was a student of Khyenrab Norbu, and made precious pills together with Amchi Kunsang Kunphen from Nyalam. He worked as a private physician in Delhi for many years, where he made his own medicines and was consulted by numerous researchers.

","

Tashi Yangphel Tashigang (bkra shis g.yang 'phel bkra shis sgang) was born in 1938, into a family of Tibetan doctors or amchi (am chi) in Nyemo (snye mo), a rural village thirty-five kilometers from Leh, Ladakh.

As a young man, he was initially trained by his grandfather, Sonam Norbu Lharje (bsod nams nor bu lha rje). In 1956, at the age of eighteen, Tashigang traveled to Tibet via the Kalimpong-Lhasa trade route and got the opportunity to further his studies at the Mentsikhang (sman rtsis khang) in Lhasa. During these turbulent years just after the arrival of the People's Liberation Army, he received teachings there from the Mentsikhang's renowned founder, Lamenpa Khyenrab Norbu (bla sman pa mkhyen rab nor bu, 1883–1962), the personal physician of the Thirteenth Dalai Lama (ta la'i bla ma 13, 1876–1933). Tashigang was in fact the first Ladakhi to be admitted at Mentsikhang's medical college.[1]

When Tashigang first arrived at the Mentsikhang he did not understand its regulations (khrims) and thought there might be problems, so he went to Chakpori instead. But the principal of Chakpori—most probably this was Tubten Tsering (thub bstan tshe ring)—encouraged him to return to the Mentsikhang and ask for help, which he did and was admitted. At the Mentsikhang, Tashigang was not an official student or a monk like most of the others. He was a private student (sger ba) like Khandro Yangga (mkha' 'gro dbyangs dga', 1907– c. 1973) and others. Private and lay tantric students (sngags pa) had no income from a home monastery or the government. Khyenrab Norbu helped them by not charging school fees, but private students still had to rely on their own or family funds, which made things difficult.

In turn, Tashigang and Karma Chopel (karma chos 'phel, 1930–1999) would accompany Khyenrab Norbu to treat poor patients along the Lingkhor once or twice a week. Tashigang also went as a substitute for Khyenrab Norbu when the latter was too busy, Khyenrab Norbu providing the medicines and/or funds for the medicines. No money was accepted from those treated. Tashigang was also helped/partly sponsored by a Ladakhi doctor named Tokpa Dawa (stog pa zla ba) who practiced in what is today the Gyabumkhang neighborhood of Lhasa. Tokpa Dawa imported Western drugs and injections to Lhasa from Calcutta. The other famous Ladakhi doctor at that time was Sonam Rinchen from Yangtang, who lived near his benefactor (sbyin bdag), the Ninety-Sixth Ganden Tripa, Tubten Kunga (dga' ldan khri pa 96, thub bstan kun dga, 1891–1964). Sonam Rinchen was officially stationed at the monastery but was also sometimes invited to treat patients in Lhasa.[2]

In the wake of the Chinese Communist invasion and the Tibetan uprising of 1959, Tashi Yangphel was shot in the leg on the way home from the college. Despite this wound, he managed to flee to India that same year. He and Amchi Lobzang Tashi from Dromo (blo bzang bkra shis), who later taught at the Men-Tsee-Khang college in Dharamsala and acted as a resident physician in Kalimpong, were two of the very few doctors who managed to escape at this early time.[3]

Tashigang said that he studied with Yeshi Dhonden in Dharamsala for roughly four years (1960–64), around the time that the Men-Tsee-Khang, then an unnamed medical institute, was built. He helped Yeshi Dhonden set up the school. At that time funds were very limited and Yeshi Dhonden and Tashigang were the first teachers, followed by Ngawang Yeshi and Trogawa Rinpoche.[4] Later more students came to study and Tashigang went to Ladakh and brought funds back from his relatives. The Ganden Tripa was another major early sponsor.

In 1960, Amchi Tashigang was appointed as one of the first resident doctors.[5] He moved to Laxmi Nagar, in the eastern suburbs of New Delhi four years later, establishing his own clinic and pharmacy, living there with his wife and three children. His son studied biomedicine and his two daughters later migrated to the United States.[6]

In the meanwhile, Tashigang joined the Delhi field office of the Library of Congress in 1968 as a Tibetan language specialist after a chance meeting with E. Gene Smith (1936–2010). Over nearly two decades of textual acquisition and cataloging under Smith's supervision, Tashi Yangphel emerged as ""the leading expert on Tibetan medical literature in exile.""[7] He traveled widely across India, Bhutan, Nepal, Tibet, and beyond to retrieve rare woodblock prints and manuscripts. After 1986 he traveled to Lhasa on many occasions to collect Tibetan medical texts and receive instructions from Jampa Trinle (byams pa 'phrin las, 1928–2011), the director of the Mentsikhang.

Tashigang had a long career in various positions of the Indian administration and contributed to the recognition of Sowa Rigpa (so ba rig pa)—the Tibetan term for the medical sciences—as a traditional medical system in exile. However, Amchi Tashigang's most significant legacy is undoubtedly his independent publication of the Smanrtsis Shesrig Spendzod series, consisting of a wide range of medical and astrological texts numbering more than 250 volumes in total, which he published between 1969 and 1989. Around eighty titles can be accessed through the Buddhist Digital Resource Center (BDRC), which Gene Smith founded in Cambridge, Massachusetts in 1999, and 144 are listed in the Library of Congress catalog. The preservation of this invaluable treasury of knowledge will continue to inspire generations of practitioners and scholars across the Himalayas and beyond. The series was generously distributed to specialized libraries and research institutes worldwide, including in the Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR), for which Tashigang received the Yuthok Award at the International Academic Conference on Tibetan Medicine that was held in Lhasa in 2000.

During an interview in 2005 (with Barbara Gerke and Jürgen C. Aschoff, in Delhi on January 5) Amchi Tashigang said that for a time he traveled to Lhasa every year to collect books. He received an invitation from the Lhasa Mentsikhang, allowing him to apply for a visa. In Lhasa he obtained special permission to xerox selected medical texts. Laughingly he remembered that among his colleagues he was known for ""asking too many questions about Tibetan literature."" His luggage contained only books and he developed an extensive collection at his home in Delhi. Until they migrated to the US, his two daughters were of great help with computerizing, editing, and collating his comments on various editions.

By 2005, he had hundreds of pages of annotated texts, but he was reluctant to publish them prematurely. At that time, he already felt that he would not be able to publish all his notes and commentaries. Tashigang himself described his work challenges to Aschoff and Gerke: ""There are editing problems. Some books that are said to be written in the twelfth or thirteenth century actually date back to the tenth century. I added the changes in brackets. I cannot correct the original; we Tibetans do not change the original texts. Grammatical errors we can change."" Apart from his tremendous achievement in publishing the Smanrtsis Shesrig Spendzod series, he left a large number of unpublished materials for future scholars. In 2005, he said: ""We need to reprint the original texts but add a twenty-first century commentary.""
Making Precious Pills

Tashigang emerged as a successful early pioneer of the private clinic-cum-pharmacy model by setting up Tashigang Herbal Centre in 1986. He became an expert pharmacist, producing, researching,[8] and exporting highly complex precious pills alongside a large number of other formulas. His wife worked alongside him and became an expert in procuring raw ingredients from Khari Baoli, Old Delhi's wholesale spice market.

Tashigang was one of the few entrepreneur physicians who obtained the skills to process mercury and make the famous multi-compound precious pills in his own pharmacy. Many precious pills contain mercury in the form of tsotel (btso thal), a black organometallic mercury-sulfide ash compound, which undergoes a long process of alchemical refinement. Making tsotel is considered the pinnacle of Tibetan pharmacology, and only a few individual physicians had been able to preserve this technique in exile.[9] Tashigang was trained in making tsotel by two of his teachers and colleagues in Lhasa and Nepal.[10] From Karma Chopel he received theoretical instructions privately while visiting Lhasa, most probably during the 1980s. Karma Chopel had taken part in making tsotel at the Powo Tramo (po bo kra mog) Chinese labor camp in Kham, in 1977, under Lamenpa Tenzin Chodrak (bla sman pa bstan 'dzin chos grags, 1924–2001) and Khenpo Troru Tsenam (mkhan po khro ru tshe rnam, 1926–2004) who processed mercury and prepared precious pills.[11]

In 1985, Tashigang received the practical tsotel transmissions from Kunsang Kunphen (kun bzang kun phan, 1924–2006) of the Nyalam region, who was taught by the medicine compounder (sman sbyor pa) Tobgyel (thob rgyal) of Lhasa Mentsikhang. In the early 1950s Kunsang Kunphen had settled in Nepal, where he treated King Tribhuvan (1906–1955) and, in 1973, established his clinic and pharmacy in Kathmandu.[12] He later built the Nyalam Medicine Factory in the TAR, which currently produces the tsotel for the precious pills made at Kunphen clinic in Kathmandu.[13] In return, some batches of precious pills are sent to Nyalam, since the factory currently does not produce precious pills itself.[14] Sometime around late 1985, Amchi Kunsang came to Delhi to make tsotel with Tashigang.[15] They were open to innovation and experimented with machinery to facilitate the grinding and burning processes until they came up with workable results, in the process also experiencing an explosion of clay pots while burning the ""eight metals"" (lcags rgyad).[16]

Tashigang went on to produce precious pills for the European market without tsotel. He also produced mercury-free precious pills for a German migraine study.[17] This involvement was based on a long-term connection with the neurologist Jürgen C. Aschoff from Ulm in Southern Germany, who recruited Tashigang. Tashigang had previously treated migraine patients with the precious pill Jumar 25, a multicompound of twenty-five ingredients, containing mercury not in the form of tsotel, but as processed cinnabar (rgya mtshal), along with pearl and lapis lazuli.[18] For the migraine study in Germany, Tashigang reformulated the pill with only thirteen ingredients, excluding all those ingredients that were not approved in Germany for human consumption. Eighteen of the twenty-two patients taking part in the open study experienced improvement with their migraine attacks after taking one pill of Jumar 13 per day for two months.[19] The precious pills he provided locally to his patients in India, however, sometimes contained tsotel.[20]

Amchi Tashigang and Amchi Kunsang Khunpen were examples of independent physicians who became entrepreneurs in the diaspora, establishing their own clinics and pharmacies, relying on their own networks, finances, and expertise to be able to produce tsotel and make precious pills. Kunsang had royal patronage from the king of Nepal, which helped him to gain recognition in Nepal, but otherwise both amchis seemed to have made their medicines outside traditional Tibetan support structures.
Scholarly exchange

Amchi Tashi Yangphel Tashigang's long friendship and collegial exchange with Dr. Pasang Yonten Arya (pa sangs yon tan arya, b. 1955) started in 1985. Pasang Yonten had studied the Smanrtsis Shesrig Spendzod published collections since the late 1970s, and two of Tashigang's nephews were his students at Men-Tsee-Khang college (1982–1986). Tashigang gifted him Yutok Yonten Gonpo's (g.yu thog yon tan mgon po, 1126–1203) biography, the Yutok Nyingtik (g.yu thog snying thig) cycle, and works on mercury purification. The two scholar-physicians discussed many more topics over the years, naturally becoming good friends as they shared insights. Pasang Yonten was inspired by Tashigang's fresh way of engaging in textual research and his wide-ranging knowledge on Ayurveda and Siddha medicine, whereas Tashigang was much impressed by his book on the history of Tibetan medicine.[21]

After many years of separation, they met again in the summer of 2013, taking ample time to delve into literature related to the Medicine Buddha (sangs rgyas sman bla). Their final meeting took place in 2017 at Amchi Tashigang's home. At that time, he had just recovered from a gallstone operation and seemed quite weak, but they were happy to be reunited. After lunch and while sharing and tasting some fresh quince fruit (bse yab, Chaenomeles speciosa), Pasang Yonten fondly remembers discussing the issue of the Tibetan identification and substitution of Indian materia medica. They then went through his impressive library once again, Tashigang donating a number of rare sources to his old friend. He also showed photographs of Medicine Buddha statues in Nepal, explaining that he had overseen the construction of a temple dedicated to the Medicine Buddha near the ancient city of Vaishali, in Bihar, where Buddha Shakyamuni is said to have expounded the Medicine Buddha Sūtra.
Over the years, many researchers of Sowa Rigpa found their way to Laxmi Nagar in Delhi to interview Tashigang and learn from his vast expertise on Tibetan medical literature.
Amchi Tashigang passed away in 2021, during the COVID-19 pandemic.
